## 6b. Parallelism — two kinds, two different tools

The extraction is ~790 independent days; the build is ~8 independent modules. Both parallelize,
but not with the same mechanism, and using the wrong one for either is expensive.

**Data extraction → a process pool, sharded by date.** Measured at 21.2 s/day, so 8 workers bring
790 days from 4.6 h to ~35–40 min. Each day is independent, writes its own
`cache/causes/YYYY-MM-DD.parquet`, and skips if that file already exists — so the job is
**resumable**, which matters more than raw speed when a CDN drops a request eight hours in.
Launched as a background `Bash` job at H0.75 and left running while everything else is built.
Shard boundaries are date ranges, so adding workers needs no coordination.

Not subagents, for the byte-crunching specifically: a pool gives backpressure, retry, and
resumability for free, costs no tokens, and 790 shards is far past the point where per-shard
agent overhead dominates. Fanning agents out over date ranges would parallelize wall-clock too,
but strictly worse on every other axis.

**Build workstreams → subagents, one per module.** This is where agents genuinely add throughput,
because the modules have clean contracts and can be written simultaneously against them:

| Agent | Owns | Contract it codes against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `entities.py`, `anchors.py`, `labels.py` | fact-cache schema; emits `entities.json`, `anchors.json`, `labels.parquet` |
| 2 | `profiles.py`, `resample.py` | fact-cache schema; emits grids per `TimelineProfile` |
| 3 | `bridge.py`, `validate.py` | the `TimeFDataset` shape; the five OpenTSLM keys |
| 4 | `discover/` tiers 0–3 | `DataSpec` in, `candidates.jsonl` + rejection table out |
| 5 | connector folders + `dataset.yaml` × 4 | TimeNet `BaseConnector`; card schema |

The two interfaces that make this safe — the **fact-cache table schema** and the
**`TimelineProfile`/`Layer` dataclasses** — get frozen and written down first, at H0.75, before
any agent starts. Everything else is behind them. `build.py` (the integrator) stays with me,
since it is where the contracts meet and where a misunderstanding would surface.

**Already written** (before re-planning, on branch `feat/db-route-multiscale`):
`causes.py` — the full 1–99 code table, six families, the QoS/placeholder exclusions, and the
regex projection, validated against the H0 measurement; and `sources.py` — URLs, the 3-hour
service-date constant, the service-group key, and the retry-configured DuckDB helper.

## 7. Leakage — three splits, and report the gap

The unit is now `(service_group, station, anchor)`, so the axes change and simplify.

- **Axis T (time)** — anchors before a boundary train, after it test.
- **Axis E (entity)** — hold out whole `(service_group, station)` pairs. Also hold out whole
  *stations* as a harder tier, since station identity leaks across every service calling there.

**Report all three cells, always:**

| Split | Disjoint in | Detects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | time only, entities shared | temporal generalisation |
| **B** | entity only, time shared | route generalisation |
| **C** | **both** | **the production number** |

**Publish C, and publish the A − C gap as the leakage estimate.** This is not pedantry: it is
precisely the difference between OpenTSLM's Sleep-CoT (random split over adjacent 30-second epochs,
69.88 F1) and ECG-QA-CoT (patient-disjoint, 32.84 F1), and reading those two as a data-volume story
rather than a split story is the mistake this plan exists to avoid. A jury that sees us volunteer
the leakage number will believe the honest one; a jury shown only the flattering number will
believe neither.

**Split A alone hides the worst failure mode.** With a 180-day context the series is effectively a
*route fingerprint*: the model learns "this delay signature is the 07:42 from Pasing" and recalls
its base rate, which is stable across a time boundary. Time-disjoint scores stay high; performance
on an unseen service collapses.

**Embargo applies to the horizon and the boundary, not the context.** Train records never see data
after the boundary. But a test anchor one week past the boundary carries a 180-day context that
overlaps the last training context by 96 %, so **insert a gap of at least one context span
(180 days) at the boundary** — purge, don't merely split. Test contexts reaching back before the
boundary are fine; that is what deployment looks like.

**Weight or cap by uniqueness.** Entities with more anchors otherwise dominate the gradient in
exact proportion to how redundant they are. Cap anchors per entity (which the staggered design
already does) or weight by average uniqueness.

**Bootstrap by entity block, not by row.** Row-bootstrap over 96 %-overlapping windows understates
confidence intervals by up to ~5×.

**Cross-profile identity** is unchanged and still guaranteed by construction: five shared,
content-hashed artifacts (`station_universe.json`, `entities.json`, `anchors.json`,
`labels.parquet`, `splits.json`) computed once before any profile is built, so `assign_split` is a
pure function of `(entity, anchor)` and identical assignment across profiles is a theorem. Every
dataset carries `artifact_bundle_sha`; the validator asserts all four match.

## 8. TimeNet contract

Verified against source, not docs — `docs/connectors.md` describes a flat-file layout the code
does not use.

**Folders — four**, `datasets/error404/db-route-{week,quarter,year,multiscale}/` each with
`__init__.py` (re-exports `CONNECTOR`), `connector.py` (ends `CONNECTOR = …`), `dataset.yaml`,
`requirements.txt`, `tests/`, over a shared internal module (~10 lines each). Discovery is lazy by
dataset id; there is no central registry to edit.

**`dataset.yaml` is JSON-Schema validated with `additionalProperties: false`** — any extra key is
a hard failure. Required: `dataset_id`, `dataset_version` (semver), `name`, `description`,
`license` (`CC-BY-4.0` is in the enum). Optional: `domains` (includes `transport`), `tags`,
`source_url`, `citation`, `access`. **Do not invent a top-level `profile:` or `leakage:` key** —
encode the profile in `name`/`description`/`tags` (`profile:S`, `bucket:1h`, `span:7d`).

**Two methods.** `download(cache_dir)` does **all** network work — the remote aggregations, the
raw-XML cause extraction, the entity enumeration — and writes the local fact cache, returning
paths. `convert(raw_refs)` reads those locally with DuckDB (local reads are not network), slices
windows, computes labels, builds tasks and annotations. Connectors take **no constructor
arguments**; the profile arrives as an env var read in `__init__`.

**Object model.** `TimeSeries.from_values(values, spec=…, signal=…, time_axis=…)`; all signals of
a modality **share one `TimeSeriesSpec`** and differ by `signal`;
`RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1, 3600))` takes a `Fraction`, not a float, deliberately.
**A record has no metadata slot** — every static fact is `Annotation(key=…, value=…)` with no
span, including `split`. **TimeNet stores archival raw**: no resampling, no normalization. All
z-scoring and padding happens later, in the load-time adapter.

**Annotations per record:** `route_id`, `origin`, `transfer_hub`, `destination`, `line1`, `line2`,
`scheduled_time_local`, `weekday`, `scheduled_recovery_min`, `route_position`, `anchor_iso`,
`window_start_index`, `imputed_fraction`, `n_horizon_instances`, `attributed_share`,
`dominant_cause_code`, `dominant_cause_text`, `step_free_access`, `mobility_service`,
`caption:<layer>/<signal>` × N,
plus the predictor scalars of § The record, which are what `pre_prompt_context` renders:
`run_delay_last3` (rank 1), `run_delay_trend_min_per_stop` (rank 1), `stops_elapsed`,
`scheduled_recovery_min` (rank 3), `habit_median_delay_8w` (rank 4), `route_position`,
`train_type` (rank 6), `is_school_holiday`, `is_public_holiday` (rank 7),
`habit_median_delay_8w` (rank 4), `train_type` (rank 6),
`pre_prompt_context`, `split`, `split_cell`, `artifact_bundle_sha`.

### Connector mechanics — verified against source, and three of them are traps

The reference implementation to copy is `datasets/timenet/hello_world/` — **five files**
(`__init__.py`, `connector.py`, `dataset.yaml`, `tests/__init__.py`, `tests/test_connector.py`;
it ships *no* `requirements.txt`). It deliberately exercises every feature, so it is the template.
TimeNet also ships an `add-dataset-connector` agent skill whose step 5 is a **hard gate**: confirm
id, source, base class, task type and a concrete example row before writing code.

**Trap 1 — `derive_schema` aborts the build on any per-key inconsistency.** The descriptor is
`(key, annotation_type, value_type, unit, description)`, and two annotations sharing a key with any
differing component raise. Concretely, all of these kill the build:
- `value=3` on one record and `value=3.0` on another → int vs float. **Cast every numeric
  annotation value at the connector boundary.**
- the same key used span-less on one record and with a span on another → **a key is one shape,
  forever.** Our dated disruption annotation therefore needs a *different key* from any static
  disruption flag.
- `unit="minute"` vs `unit="min"`, or a description present on one record and absent on another.
Set descriptions from a module-level table keyed by annotation key, and call `derive_schema()` in
our own test the way `hello_world` does.

**Trap 2 — determinism is entirely on us.** Auto-generated ids are UUIDv7, i.e. timestamped and
random, so every default id differs between builds. **Name every record, series, annotation and
task id from source keys**, and **sort every set before iterating** in `convert`. The framework
hashes its *outputs* (sha256 per file in the manifest) but never its *inputs*, and a rebuild is
skipped purely on `dataset_version` existing — nothing checks that the same version means the same
bytes. Guard with `assert_datasets_equal(_convert(), _convert())`, as all four shipped connectors do.

**Trap 3 — the docs are wrong about env vars.** `docs/connectors.md` says configuration comes from
env vars read in `__init__`; **no shipped connector does this**. Credentials are read by the client
library or inside `download()`. So the profile selector and the DB API keys are read in
`download()`, not `__init__` — which also keeps a `convert`-only unit test credential-free.
Note the live-feed corollary: if credentials change the output, two builds of the same
`dataset_version` differ. Pin a snapshot date in the card, or split into separate dataset ids.

**Smaller findings worth using:**
- `subject_ids` on `add_record` is **inert** — nothing downstream reads it (not splits, not the
  torch loader). Put the primary station id there anyway as the natural grouping key for a
  consumer's splitter, but anything that must be queryable has to *also* be an annotation.
- `target_schema` is an opaque string. The better convention (`sleep_edfx`) is to set it to the
  **id of a registered annotation holding the vocabulary**, and publish that via
  `dataset.register_annotations(...)`, so a consumer can actually resolve the label set.
- `from_tasks` chains tasks. Chain the "why" `AnswerTask` off the cause `ClassificationTask` — one
  extra field, and it is the only way the format records that they are one question at two levels.
- `requirements.txt` per connector, one comment per dependency, and **import lazily inside the
  method with a guarded `ImportError`** — an eager top-level import breaks discovery under
  `--no-isolation`.

**Build:** `timenet-build --quiet build <id> --out <dir>` (`--quiet` belongs to the tool, not the
subcommand), then `TimeNet(<dir>).load(<id>).describe()`.

**Honest tension to name in the card:** TimeNet stores archival raw, but OpenTSLM needs finite
values so imputed buckets are baked in. Store `imputed_fraction` and the imputed-bucket count per
record and state the tension rather than letting a format-literate judge find it.

## 9. Handoff into training

Our bridge is a `QADataset` subclass whose `_load_splits()` calls `TimeNet().load(dataset_id)` and
partitions by the `split` annotation. **Domain-agnostic by construction** — it reads records,
series and tasks, so any TimeF dataset can train an OpenTSLM model. That reusability is the bonus
claim, and we prove it by **loading Jonas's `error404/db-delay-hourly` through our bridge and
training one run on it**. Two independently written pipelines meeting at the format is stronger
evidence than one pipeline.

| OpenTSLM key | Built from |
| --- | --- |
| `pre_prompt` | `task.prompt` + `pre_prompt_context` annotation (route, departure, slack, cause context) |
| `time_series_text[i]` | the `caption:<layer>/<signal>` annotation **+ pre-normalization mean and std** |
| `time_series[i]` | `series.to_numpy()` → z-score per series → `list[float]` |
| `post_prompt` | the question + `You MUST end your response with "Answer: "` |
| `answer` | `task.rationale` + `Answer: {task.target}` + EOS |

**A defect in Jonas's bridge that we must not inherit.** It builds the caption from `spec.name`.
In his station dataset the three signals have three different specs, so it works. Here **four of
six series share the one `delay` spec** — all four would be captioned `"Mean delay, it has mean …
and std …:"`. At XM it is worse: the same signal appears at three timescales. Since the caption is
the **only** channel through which identity *and* scale reach the model, four indistinguishable
captions is fatal. Ours reads the `caption:<layer>/<signal>` annotation and falls back to
`spec.name` — preserving the "knows nothing about rail" property. Captions name entity and window:

> `Mean delay of ICE → Hamburg-Altona across its top-100 stops, daily over the past year, it has mean 6.2314 and std 2.1077:`

Non-negotiables, each verified in OpenTSLM source: series strictly **1-D** (multivariate = N
separate captioned series, never 2-D); z-scored **in the dataset class** with mean/std in the
caption; `time_series_text[i]` and `time_series[i]` **positionally aligned**; right-zero-padded to
a multiple of 4 with no padding mask; and `QADataset` **caches all three splits on the class at
first instantiation**, so the first `EOS_TOKEN` wins for every split.

**Model and memory.** Settled by the Gemma constraint: **OpenTSLM-Flamingo + `gemma-3-270m` +
frozen Chronos-2**, for every profile. Flamingo is flat in memory (~5.7–6.4 GB for Gemma-270M
across the paper's whole length sweep) against SoftPrompt's growth to 87 GB on 12-lead ECG, so the
multi-scale profile's OOM risk disappears and a single L40S is ample. `gemma-3-1b-pt` is the
step-up if budget allows; Llama is a drop-in if access lands.

**Nebius.** Pipeline runs locally; the built TimeF directories and the skeleton JSON go to an
Object Storage bucket the job mounts (`--volume bucket:/data --output bucket`). `injectedFiles`
(≤ 64 KiB each) carries only a bootstrap script. Do **not** stream the HF parquet from inside the
job — keep extraction local and reproducible.

## 10. The bake-off

Identical LLM (`gemma-3-270m` under Flamingo), encoder, optimizer, seed, **step count** (not epochs
— record counts are equal by construction), eval cells, generation settings.

**Pre-register the selection rule before any run, and say so in the pitch:**

> The winning profile is the one with the lowest `arrival_delay_min` MAE on **split C** (entity- and
> time-disjoint); ties broken by `late_5min` calibration (Brier) on the same cell.

And report **calibration alongside MAE**, because "will the transfer hold" is a decision, not a
regression: reliability of the predicted hold-probability in deciles, plus Brier score. A model
that is 3 minutes worse on MAE but honest about when it does not know is the more useful one, and
saying so before seeing results is what makes it a finding rather than an excuse.

Per profile: four leakage cells plus `line_unseen`, against four baselines —

1. **DB's own forecast** — the headline bar. `arrival_change_time`/`departure_change_time` is
   DB's real-time prediction and `time` is the truth, so this is computable from the archive with
   no extra source. Beating it by a few minutes of MAE, and being better calibrated on "will the
   transfer hold", is the credible win. Verify at H1 that `ct` is genuinely predictive rather than
   settled (see § Realistic ceiling); if it has collapsed onto the truth, promote persistence to
   headline and say why.
2. **Text baseline** — same numbers serialised into the prompt, no connector. Free via
   `QADataset._format_sample_str`. This is what proves the connector earns its place.
3. **Persistence / climatology** — this entity's mean delay at this hour-of-day over the context.
4. **Gradient boosting on the same scalars** — the honest tabular bar. RIDE's best deep model beat
   XGBoost by only 3.9 % on 94.5 M rail events; if we cannot clear it, that is the finding.
5. **Majority class** for the two classification tasks.
6. **Caption-only ablation** — captions kept (they carry mean and std) with the **series zeroed**.
   Almost nobody runs it and it is a credibility multiplier: **if XM's advantage survives zeroing
   the series, the "long context" benefit was never the shape — it was just knowing the annual
   mean.** That one cheap experiment directly adjudicates the hypothesis. Run it on S and XM
   before anything else optional.

Three extra rows, all cheap:

- **Recency ablation** — `HALF_LIFE_DAYS = 90` vs `∞` (uniform anchors), same everything else.
  This is the row that tests whether recency weighting earns its place, and it is the direct
  empirical answer to "does recent data deserve more weight". Run it on the winning profile.
- **Curriculum on/off** — Jonas's per-station dataset as stage 1, registered in
  `curriculum_learning.py`.
- **Cross-load interop proof** — his dataset through our bridge.

GPU is not the constraint: four runs at a few hundred LoRA steps plus eval is single-digit hours
and roughly $20–60 against a $1000 voucher. **The schedule risk is the raw-XML cause extraction
and the label distribution, not compute.**

## 10b. The monthly refresh loop — designed and documented, not built

Scoped down deliberately: a scheduler nobody can watch fire proves nothing before the deadline,
and the hours are better spent on the bake-off. It ships as a section of the dataset card and a
pitch slide, with the pipeline **built so the loop is a thin wrapper rather than a rewrite** —
which is the part that makes the claim credible rather than aspirational.

What already makes it near-free: the cause extraction is **per-day and skip-if-present**, so
extending the cache is just running it with a later end date; anchors, labels and splits are
derived artifacts keyed on `(itinerary, anchor)`; and OpenTSLM curriculum stages already resume
from the previous checkpoint.

The documented design:

1. **Detect** — poll the HF dataset's `lastModified` and tree listing for new monthly files and
   raw days. This is tier 0 of the agentic pipeline pointed at a source it already knows.
2. **Extend** — run the day shards for new dates only. Recompute anchors; the recency weights in
   §4b shift automatically because they are a function of `age_days` at build time.
3. **Detect drift, and make it the trigger** — compare the new month's cause-family mix and delay
   distribution against the training window (population stability index on the family shares).
   A new `works` regime on a corridor is exactly the signal that should force a retrain, and it
   is measurable rather than a calendar guess.
4. **Fine-tune** from the incumbent checkpoint on the new recent-only stage.
5. **Promote only on improvement** — evaluate on a rolling holdout and keep the incumbent unless
   the challenger wins. Without this gate, continual training degrades silently, which is the
   standard way these loops fail.

State honestly what is not proven: no scheduled run happens before submission, so the loop is a
design plus the primitives, not a demonstrated capability.

## 13. Sequencing (~18 h remaining)

Two people through H6. The critical move is at H0.75.

**H0 is complete** — the gate ran, `causes.py` and `sources.py` are written, the branch exists.
Clock below restarts from there; ~18 h remain.

| Window | Work |
| --- | --- |
| **H1–H1.25** | **Freeze the two contracts** — the fact-cache table schema and `TimelineProfile`/`Layer` — and write `facts.py`. Nothing else can start until these exist, so nothing else does. **Also measure `ct`-vs-actual**: is DB's own forecast genuinely predictive, or settled? It decides the headline baseline |
| **H1.25** | **Launch the sharded extraction as a background job**: 8 workers, resumable, ~35–40 min. Develop against 2026-06…08 meanwhile. **In parallel, user obtains the DB API keys** — and the moment they land, start the **5-minute IRIS archiver** for the demo corridors so it accumulates until the pitch |
| **H1.25–H3.5** | **Five subagents fan out** against the frozen contracts (§6b): entities+anchors+labels · profiles+resample · bridge+validate · discover tiers 0–3 · connector folders. I hold `build.py` and integrate |
| **H3.5–H4** | **Label + attribution distribution check.** Much lower risk now — 28 % of Munich stop events are already ≥5 min late, so the binary target is balanced without intervention |
| **H4 (parallel)** | **Wire Flamingo + `gemma-3-270m` + frozen Chronos-2.** Highest-return change available, and under Gemma it is close to mandatory — SoftPrompt scores 1.43 F1 on HAR with this base. Timebox Chronos-2; fall back to a published `-m4-` checkpoint rather than random init |
| **H4–H5** | Integrate: `build.py` wires profile → TimeFDataset. Annotations incl. `caption:<layer>/<signal>`, per-layer axis, 4 tasks, raw-template rationales, recency weights |
| **H5–H5.5** | `bridge.py` + **CPU smoke**: S and XM through collate, one forward pass on `gemma-3-270m`. Before any GPU spend |
| **H5.5–H6** | `validate.py` green: cross-profile hashes, 2025-11-02 continuity, attribution rule, phase check, `std > 1e-6` |
| **H6–H6.5** | Swap in the full fact cache; build S and XM on real L-limited anchors with recency weighting |
| **H6.5–H7.5** | **CHECKPOINT F1** — first Nebius run on S, Flamingo + `gemma-3-270m`. Proves the harness end to end |
| **H7.5–H8.5** | Build M and L; launch M. `live.py` against the now-arrived keys |
| **H8.5–H10** | *(GPU busy)* Rationale skeletons per profile, placeholder-verified, committed as JSON |
| **H10–H11** | Rebuild all four with the prose `AnswerTask` and the live-context block; revalidate |
| **H11–H13** | **The bake-off** — four profiles + the recency ablation, identical harness, same steps and seed |
| **H13–H14** | Baselines + **caption-only ablation on S and XM** + curriculum on/off + interop cross-load |
| **H14–H15** | Results table; apply the pre-registered rule; write the finding |
| **H15–H16** | Agentic tiers 0–3 + `ProfileDesigner` + the rejection table, wired end to end and re-run so the recorded decisions are genuinely its output |
| **H16–H17** | `timenet-build` all four; validate cards; connector tests; dataset cards **including the §10b refresh-loop design** |
| **H17–H18.5** | Pitch: one route, one departure, evidence at 1h/6h/1d side by side, the cause attribution, **the live disruption block**, the generated plan, the bake-off table, the rejection table |
| **H18.5–H19** | Buffer, submit |

**Fallback ladder — every rung ships:**
**F1 (H7)** S built, validated, trained on the scalar + action tasks with raw-template rationales.
**F2 (H12.5)** S + XM bake-off with the pre-registered rule — the minimum that answers the
additivity question. **F3 (H14.5)** all four profiles, full attribution of which scale mattered.
**F4** budget-matched row, per-record paraphrase, full XM signal set.

**Drop order, decided now so nobody improvises at 4am:** budget-matched row → **live layer**
(inference-only, one slide) → **L-alone** (long context still tested inside XM) → **M-alone** →
caption-only ablation on XM (keep it on S) → recency ablation (keep the weighting itself, drop
the comparison row) → prose `AnswerTask` (keep scalar + classification) → XM, ship S alone.

**Never dropped:** shared-artifact hashing, the fail-closed validator, the attribution rule,
recency weighting itself (it is a config default, not work), and one working end-to-end run.

**Hard abort is largely retired.** The per-train unit removed the itinerary-supply risk that the
abort existed for: Munich already yields 559 `(service_group, station)` pairs seen ≥20 days/month
against a recommended target of 500. If anything underruns, widen the geographic radius — the
one-hop catchment measures 8,919 qualifying pairs.

### Riskiest assumptions

Five of the original risks were retired by the H0 gate. What remains:

| # | Risk | P | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Encoder trained from scratch underperforms** | **high** | Measured in the paper at −15 F1 vs a frozen Chronos-2. Try Chronos-2 first (see *How much data*); fall back to the published `m4-sp` checkpoint. Do not random-init |
| 2 | **Five parallel agents diverge** on the shared contracts | **high, new** | Freeze the fact-cache schema and `TimelineProfile` at H1 *before* any agent starts; I own `build.py` so integration failures surface in one place; each agent ships offline tests against synthetic fixtures |
| 3 | 2025-11-02 coverage step creates a fake regime change | high if unhandled | Pinned top-100 basis; validator asserts observation-count and mean continuity across the date |
| 4 | L overfits from ~98 % context overlap between consecutive anchors | medium | Predicted in advance; report effective-independent-context count per profile; XM hedges it |
| 5 | Station/line series desynchronise by an hour | medium, **invisible** | Validator cross-correlates series 1 vs 2 and asserts peak at lag 0 |
| 6 | **Retired** — XM OOM risk was a SoftPrompt problem; Flamingo is flat in memory (~6 GB for Gemma-270M across the whole length sweep) and is now the default | — | — |
| 7 | `timenet`/`opentslm` not importable — **verified true** | certain | Pinned reproducible env before H2; `duckdb`/`numpy`/`pyarrow` already install clean on 3.12 |
| 8 | Constant series → NaN on z-scoring | medium | Validator asserts `std > 1e-6`; most likely at L where a daily cancel-rate series can be near-flat |
| 9 | **DB API keys arrive late or not at all** | medium, **new** | Live layer is inference-only and no-ops without keys. Nothing on the critical path depends on it; the archive demo still stands, minus one slide |
| 10 | **Recency weighting makes things worse** | medium, **new** | It is an ablation row, not an assumption. If uniform anchors win, that is the reported finding and `HALF_LIFE_DAYS = ∞` ships |

**Retired by the H0 gate:** cause-code recoverability and density (measured, 30.1 %); extraction
throughput (measured, ~40 min parallel); service-group key (measured, `final_destination_station`
is 100 % populated); run-key correctness (found and fixed — `(ride_id, service_date)`); itinerary
supply (measured, 39 k transfer pairs at one hub over 3 days).

### Named users, because the rubric leads with "a useful problem"

Jonas's own idea log flags that the DB direction has no named user. Name two: the **traveller with
a connection to make**, and the stronger B2B one — the **timetable planner who wants to know which
advertised connections are fiction, and why.** The cause attribution measures the second directly.

**Agentic data retrieval — TLDR**

The job: replace a hardcoded `URL = "huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/..."` with a process that *decides* what data to use, leaves evidence, and can be re-run. Nine stages. **LLMs propose, deterministic code disposes** — an LLM can suggest, never decide.

**Above the domain line (works for any dataset, any domain):**

| # | Stage | Does |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | **Scout** | Searches HuggingFace / CKAN / Zenodo / Mobilithek APIs — but scoped to *"coverage of these stations, these months"*, not "train datasets" |
| 1 | **Scorer** | Hard gates (licence, no credentials, ≥90 days, ≤1h resolution), then an LLM fills a strict JSON rubric: which stations, which months, has actual times? cancellations? cause codes? |
| 2 | **Probe** | Actually touches each survivor cheaply — parquet footer via HTTP range, 1000-row sample. Every rubric `true` gets re-checked here, so a hopeful LLM answer can't survive |
| 3 | **Schema mapper** | LLM proposes `{timestamp, entity, value, cause_code} → column names`; verified against the probe. One retry, then the source is dropped |

**Below the line (rail-specific):**

| # | Stage | Does |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | **Adapter** | DuckDB range-reads the monthly parquet over HTTPS — nothing downloaded. Plus a 5-min IRIS archiver running until the pitch |
| 4b | **Cause extractor** | Parses raw IRIS XML for cause codes + dated disruption notices |
| 5 | **Entity enumerator** | Groups into `(service_group, station)` pairs with support stats |
| 5b | **Profile designer** | LLM proposes `(bucket, span)` pairs; checker enforces ≤4096 samples, divisible by 4. **The pipeline searches over the dataset's own design** |
| 6 | **Curator** | Picks ~3,000 entities under a deterministic quota (station spread, train-type mix, disruption coverage) |
| 7 | **Rationale writer** | Paraphrases *skeletons with placeholders still in them* — ~400 LLM calls instead of 15,000, and the LLM literally never sees a number, so it cannot invent one |
| 8 | **Validator** | Fails the build closed |

**The three things that make it more than plumbing:**

1. **The rejection table.** Mobilithek → registration friction. RIS/Wagenreihung → partner contract. GTFS-RT → no history. IRIS alone → 18h horizon. A pipeline that can *reject* is the actual evidence of assessment.

2. **The probe catches a real bug.** It reports observation-count-over-time, which is how it notices piebro's station coverage jumps on 2025-11-02. Without that, the 60- and 180-day series contain a fake regime change and the model faithfully learns it.

3. **Validation is executable, not opinion.** Timestamps monotonic per run, no duplicate stop ids, planned-vs-actual sanity, coverage gaps per station — and the gating one: *is the label computable for this entity at this anchor?* Outputs a coverage report and the TimeNet card, both generated.

**Honest scoping:** this tier is **upside, not critical path** — scheduled at H15–16, after a working dataset exists. It must genuinely run and must have actually produced the recorded decisions. It does not need to sit upstream of the build at runtime.

Want me to expand any stage, or re-submit the plan?
we are using this one also, is this already accounted for? : https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data

Yes — that's the backbone of the entire plan, and it's the single most-verified thing in it. Everything I ran today was against that dataset.

**What's already in the plan about it:**

- **Primary source**, CC BY 4.0. Verified live: public, ungated, last modified today, `accept-ranges: bytes` on the resolve URL.
- **Both layers**, and we need both:
  - `monthly_processed_data/data-YYYY-MM.parquet` — 18 columns, 14.27M rows/month nationally, 595 MB per file
  - `raw_data/year=/month=/day=/` — the original IRIS XML, **the only place the cause codes survive**
- **Read strategy**: DuckDB `httpfs` range-reads it in place over HTTPS. Nothing downloaded. Measured at 62 MB/s fetch.
- **Coverage caveat baked in**: ~100 busiest stations from 2024-07, all stations only from 2025-11-02 — which is why every aggregate is pinned to a fixed station universe, or the 60/180-day series would contain a fake regime change on that date.

**Five things I measured against it today that changed the design:**

1. `train_line_ride_id` is a **daily-recurring service, not one run** (165 stops avg) — the run key is `(ride_id, service_date)`
2. Service date needs a **3-hour offset** — runs cross midnight; 99.5% → 100.0% clean stop sequences
3. `line_number` is **100% blank for ICE/IC/EC/RJ/NJ/TGV** — so the service key is `(train_type, final_destination_station)`
4. **30.1% of stops carry a cause code**; `31 Bauarbeiten` is the 5th most common
5. Its messages split into **two disjoint kinds** — per-stop cause codes (`t=d/f/q`) and dated disruption notices (`t=h`, median 22-day windows, 34% construction)

**Munich slice from it:** 529,360 stop events/month, 49 stations name-matched, **28% ≥5 min late**, 559 `(service_group, station)` pairs seen ≥20 days — against a recommended target of 3,000 pairs, so we widen the radius geographically using StaDa coordinates once your keys land.

The only source *added* alongside it is the DB API (Timetables/StaDa/FaSta) for the live layer, and that's inference-only — the trained dataset comes entirely from this archive.

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

content.text:
Draw as the engineer who has to live with the decision, not as a decorator: a diagram earns its place when it lets a cold reader see a mechanism they would otherwise have to assemble from prose - where data flows, which components talk, what changes between two options, what state a request moves through. If a sentence says it faster, write the sentence.

## What to draw

**Depict the mechanism, not its name.** A box labeled "cache" says less than the prose; the path a request takes through it, the two stores it sits between, and the arrow that disappears when the cache is removed say what the words can't. Show the parts that the argument hinges on - the boundary being crossed, the hop being added, the data that moves - and leave out the parts that don't.

**Comparing options?** Draw the difference. Two architectures side by side, a before and an after, the one edge that each option adds or removes - the reader should be able to point at what they are choosing between. A separate labeled box per option, with nothing connecting them to the system, is not a comparison; it is a restated option list.

**Match complexity to the stakes.** A one-hop question is a three-box diagram; a migration that reroutes writes through a queue needs the queue, the writer, the reader, and the ordering arrow. Draw as much as the decision actually turns on - no forced minimalism, no inventory of the whole system either.

**Label the arrows.** An unlabeled arrow is "related somehow"; `writes`, `invalidates`, `polls every 30s` is information. A legend is only worth it when the same encoding (dashed, colored, doubled) repeats; otherwise put the meaning on the mark itself.

## Inline SVG mechanics

These mechanics apply where the page renders inline SVG natively (HTML pages); a markdown-rendered page draws its diagrams in whatever fence that lane's renderer supports, and the skill that owns the lane says which. Hand-author inline `<svg>` with native shapes (`rect`, `circle`, `line`, `polyline`, `path`) and `<text>` - no libraries, no runtime, no external images.

- **Size by `viewBox`.** Set `viewBox="0 0 W H"` and let CSS scale it (`max-width: 100%; height: auto`); choose W and H for the content, not a preset. Wide flows read left-to-right; layered stacks read top-to-bottom.
- **Theme with `currentColor`.** Strokes, text, and arrowheads in `currentColor` inherit the page's foreground in light and dark themes alike; reserve a literal hue for the one element that carries meaning (the option leaned toward, the hop under discussion), and make sure it reads on both grounds.
- **Arrowheads are markers or polygons.** A `<defs><marker>` referenced by `marker-end="url(#arrow)"` (fragment-internal id) or a small `<polygon>` at the line's end - never an image.
- **Keep text legible.** Roughly 11-13px at the drawn scale, `text-anchor` for alignment, short labels (a word or three); explanatory sentences belong in the caption below the figure, not in the drawing.
- **Align to a grid.** Shared baselines and even gaps are most of what makes a hand diagram read as deliberate; eyeballed offsets read as noise.
- **One figure, one claim.** Wrap the `<svg>` in `<figure>` with a `<figcaption>` that states what the picture shows, and give the `<svg>` `role="img"` plus an `aria-label` carrying the same claim for readers who cannot see it.
- **Stay self-contained.** No `<script>`, `<style>`, or `<foreignObject>` inside the SVG; gradients, patterns, and `<use>` reference ids in the same fragment (`href="#id"`). Long decorative path data is a sign the drawing wants a real graphics tool - simplify instead.

Design plan: **IBM Plex Sans/Mono** (technical, transit-signage character — grounded in the subject), a signal-amber accent against a warm neutral, teal for "validated". Three figures: the pipeline as a structured list, the model-agnostic data flow, and the sampling lever.

# Agentic data retrieval pipeline → TimeNet → OpenTSLM
## Deutsche Bahn route planning, multi-horizon, cause-attributed

## Context

The Temporal AI Challenge (ETH Agentic Systems Lab / Aionic Labs / Nebius) asks teams to source
open time-series data, connect it through **TimeNet**, and fine-tune a **TSLM**. Two criteria are
explicitly about *data*, not modelling:

- Slide 13: *"Where useful, build an agentic pipeline to search, assess, select, retrieve, or
  validate datasets."*
- Slide 14 bonus: *"Well-chosen datasets and reusable TimeNet connectors that others can build
  on"* and *"Agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval, or
  validation of datasets are a plus."*

This plan covers that half — the pipeline ending in validated TimeNet datasets, plus the
documented handoff into training. Product question: **"suggest a realistic route plan from A to
B, grounded in the historic behaviour of the factors along that route — and say what is actually
causing the risk."** Output mirrors the organisers' flagship slide: STATE SUMMARY → RECOMMENDED
ACTION → EXPECTED OUTCOME.

Deadline **2026-09-13T10:00Z**. The H0 validation gate has already run (see below); ~18 h remain.

### Six decisions that shape everything

1. **Standalone, own branch.** A teammate (Jonas) has a working per-station-hourly pipeline on
   `origin/db-train-idea`. We do not import or edit it. We converge only at the TimeNet dataset
   boundary — and we prove that boundary holds by loading *his* dataset through *our* bridge.
2. **Multi-horizon is the experiment, not a variant.** Delay causes live at different timescales:
   rush hour is daily, construction is monthly, weather is seasonal. The pipeline is
   parameterized over a **timeline profile** and emits sibling datasets; held-out cells pick the
   winner. "We built four and let the data choose" is a result, not just a deliverable.
3. **Scale by breadth, not depth.** Nebius removes the size ceiling, but the right way to spend
   it is *more trains per station, the train ahead, disruption notices* — not older rows. Archive
   read spans ~24 months (older months exist only to supply context windows for the earliest
   anchors); **training anchors come from the last 12–18 months** (see *How much data*, which derives ~18 months of archive).
   ~500 `(service_group, station)` entities × ~16 staggered anchors ≈ 8k records × 4 tasks ≈ 32k
   samples per profile — sized to the step budget, not to the data available. Base **`gemma-3-270m`
   under Flamingo** (Llama access not approved; see *Model-agnostic data*).
4. **Delays must be attributed to a cause.** *"Not all delays happen for a reason. If there is a
   reason, the delay should happen because of this reason."* Handled in §4 — including the rule
   that stops the model inventing causality when there isn't one.
5. **Recent data outweighs old — twice over.** The profile ladder is recentred to **7 d / 60 d /
   180 d** (§5) because the timetable changes every December and a year-long window describes a
   network that no longer exists; and anchors are exponentially weighted toward now (§4b). Keep
   the two knobs distinct: **context length** is how far back one sample looks, **anchor recency**
   is which travel dates we train on. The 60-day layer is what makes "construction started last
   month, absent three months ago" visible.
6. **A live layer, now that credentials are coming.** The archive tells you the *regime*; the DB
   Timetables API tells you *today's disruptions and how long they are scheduled to last*. §4c.

---

## 0. Your scope, and what this plan already covers

Your piece of the project is deck step **02 CONNECT**. Taking its four bullets literally and
checking each against the plan:

| Deck requirement | Status | Where / what is missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *Bring the data into TimeNet* | **Covered** | §8 contract, §6 tiers 4/4b, `facts.py` → `build.py` |
| *…standardizes the **signals** (time-series)* | **Covered** | § The record — 6 hourly series + cause-family channels, shared `TimeSeriesSpec` per modality, `RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction)` |
| *…**metadata*** | **Covered, needs restating** | §8 lists the static annotations, but not as an explicit signals/metadata/annotations mapping. TimeNet has *no metadata slot*, so "metadata" = span-less `Annotation`. Worth one table so it is obviously done |
| *…**annotations*** | **GAP** | Every annotation in the plan is span-less. **We use none of TimeNet's span-bearing annotation model** — and a construction window with a real start and end is exactly what `TimeInterval` is for. See below |
| *Define the questions, labels, or targets* | **Covered, not packaged** | §Tasks defines 4. But there is no standalone question-set artifact, and "define the questions" is a deliverable in its own right |
| *Reusable connectors and ingestion pipelines* | **Mostly covered** | 4 connector folders, the domain-agnostic bridge, the tier-4 boundary, §10b refresh design. Missing: an explicit **reproducibility contract** — what a stranger running `timenet-build build error404/db-route-week` gets, and how optional credentials degrade |
| *How many months/weeks of data for training* | **GAP — asserted, not derived** | The plan says "12–18 months of anchors" without showing the work. the data-volume section below derives it |

### The annotation gap, concretely

This is the most substantive miss, and it is squarely in your scope. TimeNet's annotation model
has three shapes, distinguished only by the span:

| Shape | Span | Our use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **static** | `None` | route id, origin/hub/destination, line ids, scheduled slack, split, captions — *already in the plan* |
| **point** | `TimePoint` | a strike day, a single-day closure, a timetable-change date (the December boundary!) |
| **interval** | `TimeInterval` | **a construction period with a real start and end** |

The interval case matters because IRIS messages carry `from`/`to` validity windows, so a
`Bauarbeiten` message is not just "construction is happening" — it is a dated period we can attach
to the exact stretch of the series it covers. That turns the cause layer from a rate channel into
something the model can point at: *"works active from the 3rd to the 30th, covering 19 of the
last 60 days of this window."* It also exercises the part of TimeNet most submissions will leave
untouched, which is worth saying out loud in a connector-focused pitch.

Both mechanics are now confirmed. An interval extending beyond the record window **warns rather
than rejects**, so long construction windows are legal — and setting `Record.time_span` to cover
them removes even the warning. An hourly `RegularAxis` is a *timeline* axis, so spans are
`TimeInterval`/`TimePoint` in **microseconds**, not step indices; prefer `.micros()` over
`.seconds()` at these magnitudes to avoid float rounding.

### Measured: the archive has two disjoint message types, and we were treating them as one

Checked against 2026-08-04 raw XML, 36,006 `<m>` elements. The split is total — not a tendency:

| `t=` | n | cause code `c` | `from`/`to` | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`h`** | 17,841 | **never** | **always** | HIM **planned-disruption notice** — dated, categorised, prioritised |
| `d` / `f` / `q` | 7,762 / 7,369 / 2,824 | **always** | never | per-stop **delay cause** |
| `c` | 210 | no | no | negligible |

Three consequences, all load-bearing:

1. **`causes.py` as already written is wrong** and must be split. It reads `cat` off the same
   elements it reads `c` from, but no element carries both. Right now the `categories` field it
   returns is always empty. Two extractors, not one: `parse_stop_causes` keyed on `t ∈ {d,f,q}`,
   and a new `parse_disruption_notices` keyed on `t = "h"`.
2. **The QoS exclusion gets a second, better key.** QoS codes are 70–98 *and* carry `t="q"`
   (2,824 of them). Keying on the message type is more robust than the numeric range, and the two
   agreeing is a free cross-check the validator can assert.
3. **The interval-annotation design is confirmed, and clipping is mandatory.** Real windows:

   ```
   <m id="r2666380" t="h" from="2608030000" to="2608102359" cat="Bauarbeiten" pr="1"/>
   <m id="r2623082" t="h" from="2606060000" to="2608072359" cat="Information"  pr="3"/>
   ```
   **Median window 22.5 days, p90 64 days, max 685; 79 % exceed 7 days.** So at the S profile a
   typical construction notice *entirely spans* the 7-day context. The useful features are
   therefore not "is a notice active" but **coverage fraction of the window** and **how far into
   the notice this anchor sits** — a notice in week 1 of 9 behaves differently from week 8.
   **Correction, verified in source:** an out-of-window span is **not rejected** — TimeNet warns
   and keeps it (`warn_when_outside: bool = True`; rejection is opt-in). So do **not** clip. The
   clean move is to set `Record.time_span` wide enough to cover the disruption, which makes the
   overrun validate silently and preserves the true dates. Clipping would destroy exactly the
   information we want.

   **`Bauarbeiten` is 6,001 of 17,841 dated notices — 34 %.** The construction signal you asked
   about is not a trickle; it is a third of all planned-disruption traffic, with real dates.

**And the notices are cleanly scoped.** Measured on the same day: **every** `t="h"` element sits
*inside* an `<s>` stop element — 18,364 of them, **zero** at timetable level — so each one joins to
the processed rows through the stop `id`, which hands us station, service group, line and time for
free. But there are only **335 distinct notice ids** behind those 18,364 attachments: one notice is
broadcast across ~55 stops, 190 of the 335 touch more than one station, and the widest touches 16.

That shape is exactly right for TimeNet's annotation model. A HIM notice is a **network-level dated
event materialised onto the stops it affects**, so:

- deduplicate by notice `id` and emit **one `TimeInterval` annotation per (notice, record)**, not
  one per stop — otherwise a single construction project becomes 55 identical annotations;
- attach it to a record when the notice touched that record's station or its service group, which
  is a set-membership test on the join, not a heuristic;
- ~335 distinct notices per day network-wide means the annotation volume is trivial even across
  two years — this costs nothing to carry.

Also present and worth carrying: `pr` (priority 1 = highest … 4), `ts` (when the notice was
issued — so we can distinguish "known for weeks" from "announced this morning"), and the German
`cat` text, which is the human-readable description column.

### Scope choice worth making explicitly

The plan emits **four sibling datasets** (S/M/L/XM) from one parameterized connector. That is more
than "a connector", and it is the multi-horizon experiment rather than the CONNECT deliverable per
se. It stays because the parameterization is ~1 config object and the bake-off is the headline
result — but if the schedule tightens, **shipping one excellent connector beats four rushed ones**,
and the drop order in §13 already reflects that.

---

## What exists, verified

| Thing | State | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/agents/` | Empty placeholder, `requires-python = ">=3.10"`, `_hackos_placeholder` marker | We own it. Delete the marker or `bootstrap.sh` skips installs. Bump to `>=3.11` (TimeNet's floor) |
| `app/backend/.../training-jobs/` | Merged, working. Nebius submit/wait/logs, `gpu-l40s-a` @ $1.55/GPU-h, injected files ≤64 KiB, S3 volumes, `/outputs` | Training submission solved. Do not rebuild |
| `origin/db-train-idea` | Jonas: DuckDB extract, 168h windows, TimeFDataset builder, TimeF→OpenTSLM bridge, 2×2 leakage grid, LoRA training, 7 tests | Reference + benchmark + interop proof. Not a dependency |
| TimeNet | `github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet`, Python 3.11+. *"TimeNet hands you the data and stops there."* | Our output format |
| TimeNet→OpenTSLM bridge | **Does not exist upstream** | The reusable-connector bonus. Ours must stay domain-agnostic |
| Local toolchain | `uv` 0.11.29, pyenv 3.14.4, brew 3.12, Node 25.9, 285 GiB free. System python3 is 3.9.6 — too old | `uv python pin 3.12` |
| `timenet` / `opentslm` | **Neither importable here.** Verified | Reproducible pinned env before H2 |
| `duckdb` 1.5.5 / `numpy` 2.5.3 / `pyarrow` 25.0.1 | Install clean on 3.12. Verified | The extraction stack is ready |

**Sharpest external constraint:** OpenTSLM caps a series at **4096 samples** (1024 patches × 4)
and it is a hard `raise`, not a truncation. Hourly therefore tops out at **170 days**; hourly ×
1 year (8760) is impossible. Span and resolution genuinely trade off — which is the premise of
the experiment.

---

## Data sources

**Primary — `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`** (HuggingFace, CC BY 4.0). *Verified live during
planning:* public, ungated, last modified 2026-09-12, `accept-ranges: bytes` on the resolve URL,
`data-2026-08.parquet` = 595 MB. Two layers matter and **we need both**:

- `monthly_processed_data/data-YYYY-MM.parquet` — 17 columns incl. `station_name`, `eva`,
  `line_number`, `delay_in_min`, `time`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`,
  `train_type`, `train_line_ride_id`, `train_line_station_num`, `final_destination_station`,
  the four planned/changed timestamps, and **`id`** (unique train-stop id).
- `raw_data/year=/month=/day=/` — the **original IRIS XML** in a `response_data` column.
  **This is the only place the cause codes survive** (§4). Joins to the processed rows on `id`.
  *Verified live:* the partition exists for 2024/2025/2026, `api_name` includes
  `timetables/v1/fchg` (the endpoint that carries `<m c=…>` messages) and `response_data` is
  documented as "Raw XML or JSON response from the API". Density since **measured at 30.1 %** of
  stop elements — see the H0 gate below.

Coverage: ~100 busiest stations from **2024-07**; all stations only from **2025-11-02**.

**Secondary, optional:** gtfs.de static (`transfers.min_transfer_time` at major hubs) — but it
covers only the *next 30 days*, so it cannot describe historical service patterns and the
`stop_name` ↔ `station_name` join ("Berlin Hbf" vs "Berlin Hbf (tief)") is a 2am trap. Keep it
off the critical path; fall back to a traffic-tier constant (5/8/10 min), documented as a stated
assumption.

**In scope — credentials being obtained by the user.** All three are one login at
developers.deutschebahn.com → create an application → subscribe per API, and all send
`DB-Client-Id` / `DB-Api-Key` headers against
`https://apis.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/…`:

- **Timetables / IRIS** (free plan, 60 calls/min) — `/plan/{eva}/{YYMMDD}/{HH}`, `/fchg/{eva}`,
  `/rchg/{eva}`. ~18h forward horizon, no history. Carries **live `<m c=…>` cause messages with
  `from`/`to` validity windows** — so it says not just "construction" but *how long it is
  scheduled to last*, which the archive cannot. This is the live layer (§4c).
- **StaDa** — station accessibility: `hasSteplessAccess` (`yes`/`no`/`partial`, not a boolean),
  `hasMobilityService`, plus toilets/WiFi/lift presence. Static; call once, cache.
- **FaSta** — live elevator/escalator state per `equipmentnumber`, joined via `stationnumber`.

Keys go in `app/backend/.env` (already git-ignored) and are read from the environment. **Never
commit them**, and the connector must degrade cleanly to archive-only when they are absent —
that is what keeps `timenet-build` reproducible for anyone else.

**Rejected, and the rejection is a deliverable (§6):** Mobilithek (registration friction — the
user opted out), RIS/Wagenreihung (partner contract, not self-service), GTFS-RT (no history).

**Entities come from the observed data, not GTFS.** A `(service_group, station)` pair is a group-by
over reconstructed runs — no join, no external timetable, no name matching against another source.
