### Deduplication — hand-curated at dataset level, none below that

There is **no dedup algorithm**. The words "dedup"/"duplicate" do not appear. What exists:

> "We only include the datasets presented in Table 11 as we either hold out the other datasets, **or are already included in the Monash repository**." (Appendix A, GluonTS)

A retained overlap they disclose: *"We include the extended version of Web Traffic which **contains overlap with the original Web Traffic dataset**."* And a same-source redundancy they resolved by shrinking the *evaluation* set instead:

> "Since we use such a large amount of dataset from the same source [CalTrans PeMS], **we can no longer consider forecasting on any of these datasets as an out-of-distribution or zero-shot forecasting task anymore**, and thus omit the Traffic dataset of the LSF benchmark from our evaluations."

### Licence screening — none in the paper

The paper says **nothing** about licences. Zero occurrences of "licen*" outside arXiv's own boilerplate. LOTSA is redistributed Apache-2.0 despite absorbing Kaggle competition data, ERA5/CMIP6 and Uber TLC. If the jury asks, the honest answer is that the paper does not address it.

### Quality filtering

Two qualitative statements only: *"We take a standard approach of filtering out time series which are either too short, or have too many missing values"* (no thresholds), and a minimum of **16 time steps** ("to achieve at least 2 patches") for the short M1/M3/M4/Tourism series. Real thresholds exist only in `uni2ts` code: global GluonTS/Monash `len(target) < 20 → skip`; Favorita `length ≥ 250, missing ≤ 0.5`; Project Tycho `length ≥ 100, missing ≤ 0.25`. Missing values are kept — many sub-datasets are literally named `*_with_missing`.

### Domain balancing — §3.2.2, the ε-cap

This is the single most transferable idea in the paper.

> "**due to data imbalance across domains and frequency, we avoid sampling sub-datasets proportionately, and instead cap the contribution of each sub-dataset at ε = 0.001, before re-normalizing**: p(D_k) = ω_k / Σω_i, where ω_k = min(|D_k| / Σ|D_i|, ε)."

Two-level sampling: clipped-proportional over sub-datasets, then observation-proportional within a sub-dataset. Not uniform, not temperature-scaled — a hard cap. Effect (derived from the paper's own tables + formula): **19 sub-datasets hit the cap and together take 68.85% of sampled batches**; Buildings900K goes from 56.80% of observations to **3.62% of sampled data** (a 15.7× down-weight); Healthcare is up-weighted **36×**, Nature and Econ/Fin **36×**, Sales **10×**, Web **6×**. **There is no ablation on ε.** It is asserted, not tuned.

### Contamination control (Appendix A)

Per-source manual exclusion, not a scan. Electricity (Trindade 2015) is removed **three separate times** — from BuildingsBench, from Monash, and from ProEnFo — each time with the note "use it for out-of-distribution evaluation instead". Solar (Lai et al. 2018) likewise. Monash is ingested **train-region only** ("holding out the final forecast horizon"), CloudOps TSF pre-train-split only. BuildingsBench is the exception, ingested whole. And the honest admission (§4.2): *"the problem of comparing zero-shot methods is exacerbated by not having a standard held-out test split, making it challenging to collate a set of datasets which all the models have not been trained on."*

### Corpus ablation — one point, Table 7

| Variant | Normalized MAE | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|
| Moirai_Small (full LOTSA) | **0.655** | — |
| w/o multi patch size | 1.156 | +76.5% |
| w/o Any-variate Attention | 0.904 | +38.0% |
| **w/o LOTSA** (Monash+GluonTS only) | **0.809** | **+23.5%** |
| w/o packing | 0.785 | +19.8% |

> "We study the impact of a large and diverse dataset by training Moirai_Small **only on the GluonTS and Monash datasets**, observing that **diversity of data is critical for cross-domain training even on in-distribution evaluation**." (§4.3)

That is roughly a 27× data reduction for a 23.5% relative MAE degradation — and it **confounds volume with diversity**; the paper does not separate them. There is **no data-scaling law**, and §4.2 is explicitly agnostic on model scaling: *"The relationship between performance and model size is tenuous in this setting."*

### Heterogeneous rates and units

**Frequency → patch size**, a hard-coded heuristic (§3.1.1, Appendix B.1): yearly/quarterly → 8; monthly → 8/16/32; weekly/daily → 16/32; hourly → 32/64; minute → 32/64/128; second → 64/128. Five input and five output projection layers, shared where patch sizes overlap. Removing this is the *largest* single ablation loss (0.655 → 1.156). **Units are handled by one line only**: "(non-learnable) instance normalization (Kim et al., 2022) [RevIN] is applied to inputs/outputs." No unit metadata, no per-dataset scaler, no log transform. Residual heterogeneity is absorbed by the **mixture output distribution** (Student's t, negative binomial, log-normal, low-variance normal).

### Moirai-2 (arXiv 2511.11698, Nov 2025) — the corpus was replaced

36M series / ~295B observations, of which: non-leaking **GIFT-Eval Pretrain** (3.25M series, 230B obs); GIFT-Eval TrainTest train split; **Chronos TSMixup — 30M series, 63B obs**, K_max=4, L∈[128, 4096], *"We only use non leaking subset of datasets from Chronos data to generate the mixup to keep our training free of leakage"*; **KernelSynth — 1M series, 1.02B obs**; and ~2.15M series / 1.48B obs of **internal Salesforce CloudOps telemetry** (so Moirai-2's corpus is no longer fully open). In their ablation, the corpus swap alone bought **−8.5% MASE / −10.4% CRPS**. Also: inverse model scaling — small (11.4M) beats base (87.1M) beats large (305M).

### Real-vs-synthetic weighting (§5) — the only statement

> "We train on a mixture distribution over these datasets that aims to give sufficient weight to all granularities and datasets. The training loader samples **80% real data and 20% synthetic**, with the real data mixture providing **equal weights to the groups: hourly + sub-hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly** datasets."

So each granularity bucket gets 20% of total samples. This massively upweights small sources: weekly data is ~4.3% of the corpus by raw points but 20% of training samples. **Not stated:** how weight is split *within* a bucket (no Wiki-vs-Trends-vs-M4 ratio exists in the paper — do not invent one), where M4 quarterly/yearly are bucketed, or any per-dataset temperature/repetition factor.

### Rationale for Trends and Wiki

There is **no** claim in the paper that search/pageview data is a proxy for rich seasonality. The stated rationale is purely volume and diversity (§5): *"It is challenging to find a large time-series dataset that meets the volume and diversity of data needed for training our foundation model. We address this problem by sourcing the bulk of data used to train our models from three major sources: Google trends, Wiki Pageview statistics and synthetic time-series."* Plus one privacy note (§8): the Trends data is differentially private.

### Data ablation — one, synthetic-vs-no-synthetic (§6.2, Figure 3d)

> "we train a 200M model with **no synthetic data** added in the mix… there is a **performance drop on Monash** because many of the datasets in Monash have under-represented granularities like quarterly, yearly or 10 minutes… **almost no difference between the two models on the hourly ETTh datasets** which has a well represented granularity. However, **for the 15min ETTm datasets the model with synthetic data performs quite a bit better**."

So synthetic data's measured job is **frequency coverage**, not pattern richness. **No Trends ablation, no Wiki ablation, no 80/20 ablation.** Figure 3d prints no numbers.

### Heterogeneous granularity

Three mechanisms: equal-weight granularity buckets; synthetic data as the coverage patch; and **per-granularity context caps** — max context 512, but **256 for weekly** and **64 for ≥ monthly**, because *"we do not have sufficiently long time-series"*. Normalization: *"we use only the standard normalization part of reversible instance normalization – i.e, the context of each time-series is scaled by the context mean and standard deviation of the **first input patch**."* (The `frequency ∈ {0,1,2}` indicator on the released checkpoints appears **nowhere in the paper**; TimesFM 2.5 removed it.)

### Contamination — the weak point

Claimed (§6): *"These datasets have been intentionally held out from our pretraining data"* and, for Monash, *"even though we never trained on these datasets."*

Contradicted in two ways. Admitted (§6.1, Informer): *"**A few of these datasets are used in pretraining**, so we focus on the other datasets in this collection (ETTm1, ETTm2, ETTh1 and ETTh2)."* Unadmitted and arithmetically verifiable: Monash `traffic_hourly` is **862 series × 17,544 steps = 15,122,928 points** — bit-for-bit the "Traffic / Hourly / 862 / 15,122,928" row of Table 1, and it is one of the 18 Monash evaluation datasets. There is no temporal cutoff argument anywhere, and contamination is **not** listed among the paper's limitations.

### Later versions (no papers exist)

TimesFM 2.0 (500M, context 2048) added *"a subset of the LOTSA pretraining data"* — 20 named datasets — with **no size or weights disclosed**. TimesFM 2.5 (200M, context 16k) re-based off LOTSA onto **GIFT-Eval Pretrain** + Wikimedia (cutoff Nov 2023) + Trends (cutoff EoY 2022) + *"Synthetic and augmented data"*. TimesFM 3.0 (330M, Aug 2026, non-commercial weights) claims *"more than **1 trillion time points**"* and is the first to state a decontamination step: *"GiftEvalPretrain **excluding the datasets that overlap with fev-bench**."*

### The scarcity argument — the quotes you want

**Abstract:** *"Pre-training large models on time series data is challenging due to (1) **the absence of a large and cohesive public time series repository**, and (2) diverse time series characteristics which make multi-dataset training onerous."*

**§3.1, the money quote:** *"**Unlike natural language processing and computer vision, where large-scale datasets such as The Pile and ImageNet-1K are easily available for pre-training, public time series datasets are much smaller, scattered, and largely task-specific.** To bridge this gap, we collate multiple time series from 4 task-specific, widely-used public repositories…"*

**Introduction, C2:** *"Unlike text and images, which have largely consistent sampling rates and number of channels, time series frequently vary in their temporal resolution, number of channels, lengths, and amplitudes, and sometimes have missing values. As a result, **large-scale mixed dataset pre-training is largely unexplored**."*

**Related Work:** *"**all existing time series models are (pre-)trained and fine-tuned on individual datasets**, and the benefits (or drawbacks) of large-scale multi-dataset pre-training remains unexplored."*

Two precision notes for the jury: the paper **never uses the words "proprietary", "scarce", "scarcity", or "fragmented"** — the vocabulary is *"much smaller, scattered, and largely task-specific"*. And §4.3 actually cuts against a pure-scarcity reading: *"there is **sufficient** publicly accessible pre-training data available in the Time Series Pile to facilitate pre-training time series foundation models from scratch."*

### Aggregation, splits, contamination

**No deduplication** — zero occurrences of "dedup"/"duplicate", and Electricity/Traffic/Weather each appear in *both* the Informer table and the Monash table at **identical observation counts** (Traffic hourly = 15,122,928 in both), so the 1.13B total double-counts.

Splits (§3.1, Figure 2 caption): *"We adhere to the predefined splits provided by the creators of each dataset. In cases where such splits are unavailable, we randomly sample **60% for training, 10% for validation, 30% for testing**… **We only use the training splits of all datasets for pre-training.**"* Long series split **horizontally** along time; short series assigned **whole** to one split. Same random seed (13) throughout, *"thus ensuring that MOMENT only observes the training splits of datasets during pre-training."* This is the cleanest contamination statement of any of the five papers.

Preprocessing: fixed **T = 512**, N = 64 patches of P = 8, **RevIN** per instance, strict **channel independence**, longer series sub-sampled (stride unspecified), shorter series **left-padded with zeros**, and a patch is replaced by a learnable `[MASK]` embedding if **any** of its 8 steps is unobserved. Temporal resolution deliberately not modeled: *"this information is often unavailable outside of time series forecasting datasets."*

### No data-scaling result

**The lineage audit.** arXiv 2510.13654 ("Rethinking Evaluation in the Era of Time Series Foundation Models: (Un)known Information Leakage Challenges") traced the dataset lineage of **22 peer-reviewed TSFMs** published through January 2026:

> "Once a dataset has been used for pre-training or fine-tuning by any model, it must be regarded as contaminated and is no longer admissible for TSFM benchmarking… **only 6% of the analyzed datasets have never been used for pre-training or fine-tuning**, making them the only suitable candidates for genuine zero-shot model benchmarking."

**How much leakage is worth.** GIFT-Eval (arXiv 2410.10393) App. F.2 is the canonical ablation — they pretrained Moirai on their clean split and compared against the original Moirai whose corpus contained ~0.1% of the eval data:

> "**In most cases, data leakage from training sets can boost performance on the corresponding test sets, with this effect becoming more pronounced as prediction length increases.** This finding highlights the **capacity of foundation models to memorize training data**."

Re-analysed in 2510.13654: at short horizons the leaked model has on average **7.6 percentage points lower MAPE**; at medium horizons **32 pp**; at long horizons **29 pp**. And **larger models are more susceptible** — the biggest gap is Moirai-L vs Moirai-Leakage-L.

**Indirect leakage — the one that will actually bite you.** 2510.13654 §3.2 identifies a failure mode specific to globally-trained models: *"if training and test series **overlap temporally and have a causal relationship** (confounding or direct causation), such pattern transfer can result in information leakage."* Two measurements:

- **Rodrigo & Ortiz (2024):** metro, bus, road and train usage in Madrid, 2024. Two globally-trained models, both predicting only the held-out metro test period. Model A had a common train/test cut across all series; model B cut only the metro series and kept the *other correlated series whole* in training. **MAE 439.14 (clean) vs 248.24 (leaky) — a 43.47% improvement from indirect leakage alone**, with no direct access to the target series.
- **Their own replication** with a from-scratch Time-Series Transformer: only **7 series out of 484 (1,600 of 205,859 observations = 0.78%)** temporally overlapped the COVID test window. The leaky model still won 8 of 10 seeds, with **up to ~37% MAE difference during the shock**.

**Their recommended standard** (§4) is two-dimensional, and it is exactly the standard I'd hold your corpus to:

> "Unlike local models, TSFMs learn patterns globally. Consequently, **strict temporal ordering within a single time series is no longer sufficient** to guarantee a fair evaluation… **if the last pre-training timestamp across all evaluated models is t, only observations from t+1 onwards can be present in the test set.**"

**Current practice.** fev-bench (arXiv 2509.26468) reports a per-model **self-reported Leakage (%)** column — in Chronos-2's Table 3: Moirai-2.0 **28%**, TimesFM-2.5 **8%**, Toto-1.0 **8%**, TiRex 1%, Sundial 1%, and Chronos-2 / Chronos-Bolt / TabPFN-TS / COSMIC / the statistical baselines **0%**. ## 7. The transfer question — answered explicitly

I read your `db_route` pipeline to answer this concretely rather than generically. Your setup: **`DEFAULT_TARGET = 3000` entities × M=5 anchors = ~15,000 samples**; entities are (service group, station) pairs over a six-region catchment from `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` (CC-BY-4.0); 6–10 signal channels per sample; four sibling profiles S/M/L/XM differing only in context length; targets `departure_delay_min` and `late_5min` (18.9%–28% positive); model is OpenTSLM (arXiv 2510.02410), LoRA on an LLM backbone with a time-series encoder.

### What does not transfer — be blunt about this

**TSMixup does not transfer, and its own ablation says so.** Three independent reasons:

1. **Chronos measured the in-domain effect and it was nil.** *"The model trained on TSMixup augmentations obtains **similar in-domain performance** to the model trained without augmentations. However, the **zero-shot** performance improves."* Your evaluation is entirely in-domain. You would be buying the one thing you don't need.
2. **The mechanism requires cross-dataset diversity you don't have.** Algorithm 1 line 6 samples a *dataset index* uniformly from N_d=28 datasets. With one archive, N_d = 1, and TSMixup degenerates into averaging pairs of German rail delay series — which is not a new pattern, it is a smoothed old one. Iwana & Uchida's variance correlation (§7.2.4) predicts exactly this: augmentation helps least when the dataset variance is low.
3. **It would break your label.** Your labels are functions of `(entity, anchor)` and your `assert_no_horizon_leak` invariant depends on that binding. A convex combination of two entities' histories has no coherent target, no coherent `ctx_*` slot, and no defensible rationale text. You would have to fabricate a label for it, and the resulting sample would teach the model to hallucinate.

**KernelSynth does not transfer either, for a different reason.** Its measured job in TimesFM was **frequency coverage** — *"there is almost no difference between the two models on the hourly ETTh datasets which has a well represented granularity"*. You have one archive at fixed resolutions you control. There is no under-represented frequency for GP samples to fill. And note the optimum in Chronos was **10%** with performance degrading above it — at your scale, 10% of 15,000 is 1,500 GP samples, which is far too few to change a 1B-parameter LoRA fine-tune and far too many to be harmless if they're off-distribution.

**The Salesforce synthetic-data survey (arXiv 2503.11411) states the position directly.** Its TSFM section has subsections for synthetic data in *pretraining* and in *evaluation* — and **no fine-tuning subsection at all**. Its §3.3 lists this as an open problem:

> "**Missed Opportunity to Finetune with Synthetic Data.** The focus on synthetic data has almost exclusively been on **pretraining**, while finetuning **remains an untapped potential**. After a TSFM is pretrained, finetuning with carefully designed synthetic data could serve as a precise intervention…"

So: synthetic augmentation for a single-domain fine-tune is not a proven technique the field endorses. It is a **stated research direction with no published evidence behind it**. If you do it, you are running the experiment, not applying a result. That is a defensible thing to say to a jury — and a much better answer than pretending Chronos validated it.

**Also irrelevant at your scale:** LOTSA's ε=0.001 sub-dataset cap (you have one dataset), TimesFM's granularity buckets (you fixed your resolutions), Moirai's per-frequency patch projections (OpenTSLM has one patch size, 4), and every observation-count figure in sections 1–5. Do not let anyone anchor you to 84B or 27B; those are pretraining budgets for a different problem.

**Two augmentations you might reach for that the evidence says will actively hurt:** permutation (destroys the trend and the timetable-week structure your L/XM profiles exist to capture — 5/6 models degraded in Iwana & Uchida) and flipping/rotation (**6/6 models degraded, 5 significantly** — and a negated delay series is physically meaningless). Time warping also degraded 5/6 and would distort exactly the weekday periodicity your `ANCHOR_STRIDE_DAYS = 7` grid was designed to preserve.

**1. The 10-to-1 rule: entity diversity, not sample count.** Your own `anchors.py` derivation is correct and is the strongest quantitative argument you have. With intra-entity ρ ≈ 0.20 and the standard design effect `n_eff(M) = M/(1 + (M−1)ρ)`:

| M anchors/entity | n_eff | marginal |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.000 | — |
| 5 | 2.778 | 0.278 |
| 6 | 3.000 | **0.222** |
| 10 | 3.571 | 0.110 |
| ∞ | 5.000 | 0 |

Your 15,000 nominal samples are **~8,333 effective independent samples**. And a **fresh entity is worth 2.778 effective samples; a sixth anchor on an existing entity is worth 0.222** — a fresh entity is **12.5× more valuable**. Every augmentation you could build sits *below* the extra-anchor line, because an augmented copy of an existing entity has ρ ≈ 1 with its source, not 0.2. **The marginal-value question answers itself at your scale: breadth beats everything.** Your existing quota (`MIN_STATIONS=25`, `MAX_PER_STATION=30` forcing ≥100 stations, `MAX_TYPE_SHARE=0.40`, `MIN_AFFECTED_SHARE=0.20`) is the right instrument, and it is the direct analogue of Moirai's ε-cap — a hard cap converting a size target into a breadth requirement.

**2. Meanwhile the **quality** filter was worth 0.5 points on a 6-point scale, and **diversity** (heterogeneous Stack Exchange prompts vs homogeneous wikiHow "how-to" prompts) *"yields significantly higher performance"*. Their conclusion: *"the scaling laws of alignment are not necessarily subject to quantity alone, but rather a function of **prompt diversity while maintaining high quality** responses."* Your model is an LLM with a LoRA adapter. This is the literature that governs you, not the pretraining-corpus literature.

At 15,000 samples the binding constraint is **epochs-to-overfit, not sample count**, and the remedies are early stopping and LoRA rank — both far cheaper than synthesizing data.

**4. The adaptation-strategy result, which depends on model scale.** arXiv 2607.23146 evaluated zero-shot / FFT / LoRA-FullShot / LoRA-FewShot across GIFT-Eval:

> "For Chronos 2, zero-shot performance is strongest on **small datasets** (MWQL_n = 0.423), where **all fine-tuning strategies degrade performance** — full fine-tuning in particular, which increases MWQL_n to **0.577**. This suggests that small datasets provide insufficient data to adapt Chronos 2's 120M parameters without overfitting, **even with LoRA**."
> "the optimal adaptation strategy depends on model scale: **LoRA-FullShot is the most effective approach for Chronos 2, while FFT is better suited to TTM (a compact model)**."
> "FFT is **unreliable** for Chronos 2, consistently degrading performance across most settings, which underscores the risk of overfitting when fully updating a large pre-trained model on limited downstream data."

Your fine-tune is worth doing (Lag-Llama: rank 6.714 → 2.786; TTM 10% few-shot flips a 2–7% deficit into a 4–9% surplus). And **more epochs and more data both erode the pretrained model's advantage**, so if your bake-off shows S/M/L/XM converging, that is the expected shape, not a bug.

**6. The break-even numbers, which you should quote pre-emptively.** arXiv 2607.04919, 30 datasets, Chronos/Moirai/Lag-Llama zero-shot and LoRA vs Naive/ETS/ARIMA/XGBoost at six training fractions: FMs win at every fraction on **15/30**; classical methods overtake at as little as 2% of data (**21–2,768 samples**) on 6/30; break-even ranges **24 to 8,361 samples** on the remaining 9. Their Finding 2: *"LoRA improves over zero-shot on **17 of 30** datasets at full training data, but gains are uneven… On short series, fine-tuning **further degrades** performance (ILI, 966 total samples: Chronos-Bolt-S ZS 2.472, LoRA 2.766). The common assumption that fine-tuning generally improves over zero-shot **does not hold unconditionally**."* At ~15,000 samples you are **above** every break-even they measured — so a jury is entitled to ask whether a gradient-boosted baseline on your `ctx_*` features beats your TSLM on the numeric target. **Run that baseline before the pitch.** You will either have a strong result or you will avoid a bad question.

**7. Frequency-domain augmentation, if you augment at all.** It is the only family with a shipped precedent in this exact literature (Lag-Llama §4.5: Freq-Mix + Freq-Mask, p=0.5, mask rate 0.5, mix rate 0.25) and the only one that leaves the amplitude spectrum — your seasonality — intact. **Window slicing and window warping** are the two time-domain methods Iwana & Uchida actually recommend, and window slicing is nearly free for you: it is the same operation as varying `context_days`, which your S/M/L/XM ladder already does as a controlled experiment. Treat that ladder as your augmentation study and report it as one.

**8. One thing to stop doing.** `repeat_count()` oversamples recent anchors by up to `REPEAT_MAX = 4` via **exact duplication**. The rationale (tilt toward the current timetable) is sound; the mechanism is the one thing LM fine-tuning literature is clearest about. Lee et al. 2021 (arXiv 2107.06499): deduplicated models *"emit memorized text **ten times less frequently**"*, *"over 1% of the unprompted output of language models trained on these datasets is copied verbatim"*, and dedup lets models *"require fewer train steps to achieve the same or better accuracy"*. A 4× duplicated sample in a 15,000-sample LoRA fine-tune with up to 200 epochs is 800 exposures of one rationale string. **Use a per-sample loss weight instead of a repeat count** if OpenTSLM's collate allows it; if it does not, cap `REPEAT_MAX` at 2 and say why.

### Direct answer on synthetic augmentation

**No, do not do TSMixup/KernelSynth-style synthetic augmentation for this fine-tune.** It is a pretraining-only trick in every published result: Chronos measured its in-domain contribution at zero, TimesFM measured its contribution as frequency coverage you don't need, and the Salesforce survey lists fine-tuning with synthetic data as an *unexplored opportunity* rather than a validated technique. Spend the same effort on entity breadth, where your own arithmetic says the return is 12.5× higher per unit of work.

The one genuinely promising synthetic-adjacent move — and the one your model's own paper measured — is **not** synthesizing data. It is **swapping in a pretrained time-series encoder**. OpenTSLM Table 3: using pretrained Chronos-2 as the encoder inside OpenTSLM-Flamingo improved **Sleep-CoT F1 from 49.33 → 64.57** (Llama3.2-1B) and **51.38 → 68.33** (Gemma3-270M), and TSQA accuracy **77.86% → 99.69%**. Those are 15-point F1 gains on the *smallest* CoT dataset in their suite — larger than anything any augmentation in this entire literature has ever produced. That is where a pretrained corpus of 10¹¹ observations reaches you: through the encoder weights, not through your data pipeline.

*(One caveat if you take that route: Chronos's tokenizer represents `[−15s, +15s]` where `s` is the mean absolute value. A delay channel with mean ≈ 4 min covers ±60 min and clips beyond that; your `works_share` and `*_share` channels are bounded in [0,1] with small means and will lose precision. Chronos §5.7 recommends standardization instead of mean scaling for such series.)*

## 8. The one thing to steal

**Not an augmentation. The two-dimensional held-out grid — and publishing the gap between its cells.**

The single most consequential finding in this literature for a project like yours is arXiv 2510.13654 §3.2: for globally-trained models, **a correct temporal split is not sufficient**. If your test entities share a time period with your training entities, and those entities are causally coupled, the model can learn the shock from one and reproduce it on the other with no direct access to the target. The measured effect sizes are not marginal: **43.5% MAE** in the Madrid transport experiment (metro/bus/road/train, one city, one year — structurally identical to your setup), and **up to 37%** in their own replication where only **0.78% of observations** temporally overlapped.

German rail is the worst case for this. Knock-on delay propagation is not a confounder you might have — it is a channel you explicitly compute (`knock_on_share`). Two entities at the same junction on the same afternoon are not independent observations; they are two views of one disruption.

**You have already built the right instrument, and it is currently switched off.** `plan_anchors(split_mode=...)` supports `"temporal"`, `"entity"` and `"both"`, and `"both"` emits exactly the four cells the literature calls for — `train`/`val`, `test_seen_entity` (later date, seen entity = temporal generalization), `test_seen_time` (unseen entity, seen date = route generalization), and `test` (both held out). Your own comment already states the case: *"the gap between `test_seen_entity` and `test` is the memorisation estimate, and publishing it is what makes the headline number believable."* But the default is `"temporal"` and the CLI's `--split-mode` only exposes `("temporal", "entity")` — `"both"` is unreachable from the command line.

So, concretely:

1. **Add `"both"` to the `--split-mode` choices and make it the default for the run you present.** It is a one-token change to an `argparse` line.
2. **Report all four cells in the deck, with `test` (cell C) as the headline.** Chronos-2's phrasing is the template: state that the corpus does not overlap the test portion at any resolution, and disclose the partial overlap that remains. fev-bench institutionalises this as a per-model `Leakage (%)` column; GIFT-Eval ships a whole separate non-leaking pretraining corpus for it. A jury that sees four cells and a stated memorization gap will trust the headline number. A jury that sees one number will ask how you know it is real, and "we split by date" is — per this literature — **not a sufficient answer for a globally-trained model**.
3. **Expect `test_seen_time` (cell B) to be optimistically biased and say so.** One caveat about your implementation: in the `"both"` branch, `purged()` returns `False` for held-out entities, on the reasoning that *"a held-out entity shares no label with training whatever its date, so the date boundary is the only place a horizon can leak across."* That reasoning is exactly the assumption 2510.13654 §3.2 falsifies for global models. Cell B is the Madrid configuration. It doesn't need a code fix — cell C is your production number and it is correctly constructed — but it needs a sentence in the deck, because someone will ask why cell B looks better than cell C, and "indirect leakage via network-wide shocks, measured at 37–43% elsewhere in the literature" is a much better answer than a shrug.

**Why this and not something about the data itself:** every corpus decision you can still make at this hour moves your metric by a few percent. This one determines whether the metric means anything. Chronos, Moirai, TimesFM and MOMENT all had to shrink their *evaluation* sets after the fact because their corpora had absorbed the test data — TimesFM still ships a Monash evaluation containing a dataset that is bit-identical to a row of its own Table 1, and only 6% of public time-series datasets remain clean enough for honest zero-shot benchmarking. You have the rare luxury of one archive, full provenance, and a splitter that already implements the state of the art. Turn it on.

# THE DEFENSIBLE POSITION

At 10³–10⁴ single-domain windows, fine-tuning a pretrained forecaster: skipping data augmentation is well-supported. The published forecasting evidence says (a) time-domain augmentation — jitter, scale, warp, permutation, DBA/ASD, MBB — is net **harmful** (FrAug 21/24 degraded; Dominant Shuffle ASD 50/72 and MBB 51/72 degraded); (b) synthetic augmentation hurts **67% of trials** and is architecture-conditional (2605.06032); (c) the papers reporting large gains used weak baselines (STAug on Informer) and those gains **invert** against modern models; (d) the wins that survive — frequency-domain masking/mixing — are ~5% MSE and were validated at **1% data**, not your regime; and (e) GP-synthetic and mixup have only ever been shown to pay off **at pretraining scale**, where Chronos's own sweep caps the benefit at ~1–7% relative and shows it **degrading past ~10–20% mixing**. If you are later pushed to add one thing, the evidence points to frequency-domain FreqMask/FreqMix or dominant-frequency shuffle — not mixup, not GP-synthetic, not DBA.

### KernelSynth — §4.2, Algorithm 2, Table 2 (kernel bank)

Inverse of the Automatic Statistician (Duvenaud et al. 2013): rather than searching kernel space to explain a series, compose kernels at random and sample from the prior.

- **Kernel bank 𝒦 (Table 2), 5 families:**
  - Constant: `κ = C`, C = 1
  - White noise: `κ = σₙ·1(x=x')`, σₙ ∈ {0.1, 1}
  - Linear (trend): `κ = σ² + x·x'`, σ ∈ {0, 1, 10}
  - RBF (smooth local variation): `κ = exp(−‖x−x'‖²/2l²)`, l ∈ {0.1, 1, 10}
  - Rational quadratic: `κ = (1 + ‖x−x'‖²/2α)^(−α)`, α ∈ {0.1, 1, 10}
  - Periodic: `κ = exp(−2sin²(π‖x−x'‖/p))`, **p ∈ {24, 48, 96, 168, 336, 672, 7, 14, 30, 60, 365, 730, 4, 26, 52, 6, 12, 40, 10}** — i.e. hand-picked seasonal periods for hourly/daily/weekly/monthly/quarterly data.
- **Composition:** sample `j ~ U{1, J}` kernels i.i.d. with replacement, **J = 5**; fold them left-to-right with a uniformly random binary operator `⋆ ∈ {+, ×}`.
- **Sampling:** draw one series of length **l_syn = 1024** from `GP(0, κ*)`.
- **Volume: 1M synthetic series.** (The Salesforce synthetic-data survey, arXiv 2503.11411 Table 3, tallies Chronos's synthetic contribution as **512M observations**, marked "PT (Mixed)".)

### The mixing ratio and the ablation (§5.2, §5.6, Figure 10b)

> "We sampled time series from the augmentations and synthetic data in the ratio **9:1** during training."

The ablation swept 0% → 100% synthetic on Chronos-T5 (Small, 46M):

> "Both in-domain and zero-shot metrics improve with the incorporation of synthetic data. **The most consistent improvement is observed around the 10% synthetic data proportion. Further increasing the proportion of synthetic data tends to worsen performance.** This is unsurprising since the synthetic data generated using Gaussian processes is not representative of all real-world time series."

And the synthetic-only model:

> "While the model trained only on synthetic data performs worse relative to models with real data in their training corpus, it performs reasonably well in terms of its absolute performance… it performs significantly better than ForecastPFN… Surprisingly, it also outperforms several other baselines in our benchmarks, despite never having seen real data during training."

**Training config for context:** T5 Mini/Small/Base/Large (20M/46M/200M/710M) + GPT-2 (90M); batch 256; context 512, prediction 64; vocab 4096 uniform bins over `[−15, +15]` after mean scaling; 200K steps, AdamW, LR 1e-3 → 0 linear, wd 0.01; 8× A100-40GB.

**Fine-tuning (§5.5.2, Figure 6)** — relevant to you: Chronos-T5 (Small) fine-tuned per-dataset, **dataset-agnostic, LR 1e-3 annealed linearly to 0 over 1,000 steps**, moved from mid-pack zero-shot to **top of Benchmark II overall**, beating both larger zero-shot Chronos variants and every task-specific model. A 1,000-step fine-tune. That is your budget order of magnitude.

**Two limitations that bite for delay data (§5.7):** (a) tokens span `[−15s, +15s]` where `s` is mean absolute value, so sparse/spiky series overflow the representable range and low-variance/high-mean series lose precision — delay series are exactly the spiky, right-skewed, near-zero-mode shape that stresses this; (b) Chronos underestimates trend with short context and struggles with exponential trend.

### Chronos-2 — arXiv 2510.15821, §4 and Appendix A

The direction of travel is unambiguous: **more synthetic, not more real.**

> "For a generalist pretrained model such as Chronos-2, the training data often plays a more decisive role than the model's specific architecture. Although recent efforts have expanded the availability of large-scale time series datasets, they primarily contain univariate data. To overcome this limitation and endow Chronos-2 with in-context learning capabilities, **we relied extensively on synthetic data**." (§4)

- **Univariate real (Table 6, 19 datasets):** Electricity, KDD Cup 2018, M4 (D/H/M/W), Mexico City Bikes, Pedestrian Counts, Solar, Taxi, Uber TLC, USHCN, Weatherbench, Wiki, Wind Farms, Temperature-Rain, London Smart Meters, Alibaba/Azure/Borg cluster traces, LargeST, Q-Traffic, Buildings 900K. Drawn from the Chronos and GIFT-Eval pretraining corpora.
- **Two new univariate generators:** **TSI** (random trend + seasonality + irregularity composition, after Bahrpeyma et al. 2021) and **TCM** (temporal causal model — sample a random causal graph, generate by autoregression).
- **Multivariate / covariate-informed: 100% synthetic.** "Multivariatizers" take series from base univariate generators (AR, ETS, TSI, **KernelSynth**) and impose dependencies — *cotemporaneous* (instantaneous correlation) or *sequential* (lead–lag, cointegration).
- **Ablation (§5.4, Figure 8b):** Chronos-2-Synth, trained on **synthetic only**, "performs only slightly below the version with real data" on Benchmark II and GIFT-Eval; a larger gap on fev-bench. Conclusion: *"with further research, real data may not even be required for effective pretraining."*
- Base model 120M; a 28M variant lags by **~1 percentage point of skill score** on GIFT-Eval at ~2× the speed. Context 2,048, post-trained to 8,192.

**Decontamination statement (§5.1) — steal this wording:**

> "When constructing the pretraining corpus for Chronos-2, we carefully ensured that it **did not overlap with the test portions of any GIFT-Eval task at any sampling frequency**. Nonetheless, the corpus does include partial overlap with the **training portions** of some GIFT-Eval datasets."

from line 370
## 6. Cross-cutting techniques

### 6a. Which augmentations help and which hurt

**Iwana & Uchida, PLOS ONE 2021 (arXiv 2007.15951)** — 12 augmentation methods × 6 architectures × **all 128 UCR datasets**. Average accuracy with paired t-tests against no augmentation. I extracted Tables 1–3 in full and tallied them:

**Of the 72 (method, model) cells, 44 (61%) had a *negative* mean accuracy change. 23 cells were significantly worse (p < 0.1); only 10 were significantly better.**

Per method, count of models (out of 6) where the effect was negative:

| Method | Negative | Sig. worse | Sig. better |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Rotation / flipping** | **6/6** | **5** | 0 |
| Permutation | 5/6 | 2 | 0 |
| **Time warping** | 5/6 | **4** | 1 |
| Magnitude warping | 4/6 | 2 | 0 |
| SPAWNER | 4/6 | 2 | 2 |
| wDBA | 4/6 | 2 | 0 |
| RGW | 4/6 | 1 | 0 |
| Jittering | 3/6 | 2 | 0 |
| **Window slicing** | 3/6 | 1 | **2** |
| Scaling | 2/6 | 1 | 0 |
| **Window warping** | **2/6** | 1 | **3** |
| **DGW** | **2/6** | **0** | **2** |

The authors' own summary: *"**Slicing, Window Warping, and DGW tended to have the most positive effects** for each model while **Rotation, Permutation, and Time Warping had significantly degraded accuracies**."* And their recommendation: *"As a general, easy-to-use, and effective method, the **Window Warping** algorithm… is the most recommended… In addition, **slicing**, i.e., window slicing… also showed to be very effective in most cases."*

**Why rotation and permutation fail is principled, not incidental.** Rotation/flipping: *"rotating a time series can change the class associated with the original sample"* — it destroys sign and direction semantics. Permutation: *"permutation does **not preserve time dependencies**"* — it destroys trend and long-range structure by construction. Both are image-augmentation intuitions that do not survive the transfer to sequences.

**Architecture dominates the augmentation choice.** Per model, negative cells out of 12: **LSTM-FCN 12/12 (10 significantly worse)**, MLP 10/12 (6 sig. worse), BLSTM 9/12, ResNet 7/12, LSTM 5/12, **VGG 1/12 (5 significantly better)**. Choosing the wrong architecture/augmentation pairing is worse than not augmenting at all.

Exact hyperparameters used, so you can reproduce or cite them: jittering σ = 0.03; scaling μ=1, σ=0.2; magnitude warping cubic spline, 4 knots, μ=1 σ=0.2; permutation 2–5 equal segments; slicing crops to 90% then interpolates back; time warping cubic spline 4 knots; window warping takes a random 10% window and warps time by 0.5× or 2×.

**For forecasting specifically** — Wen et al., IJCAI 2021 (arXiv 2002.12478), Table 3, DeepAR and Transformer with cropping + warping + flipping + APP:

| Dataset | DeepAR w/o → w/ | Transformer w/o → w/ |
|---|---|---|
| electricity | 0.87 → 0.97 | 1.04 → 1.11 |
| **traffic** | **0.66 → 0.80** | **0.70 → 0.91** |
| m4-hourly | 6.33 → 5.35 | 7.77 → 7.87 |
| m4-daily | 4.88 → 4.48 | 7.85 → 7.38 |
| m4-weekly | 12.00 → 9.34 | 6.62 → 7.09 |

(MASE, lower better. The paper's ARI column is internally inconsistent with these raw values on the electricity row — cite the raw MASE.) The pattern is the point: augmentation **hurt** on the two large, dense, long-series datasets and **helped substantially** on the M4 sets of many short series. The authors' own hedge: *"the data augmentation methods bring promising results for all models in average sense. **However, the negative results can still be observed for specific data/model pairs.** As a future work, it motivates us to search for advanced automated data augmentation policies that stabilize the influence of data augmentation specifically for time series forecasting."*

**Frequency-domain augmentation** is the one family with a decent track record and it is what Lag-Llama actually shipped (Freq-Mix / Freq-Mask, Chen et al. 2023, at p=0.5). Wen et al. cover **APP** (amplitude and phase perturbation — random phase shuffle in the phase spectrum after Fourier transform) and AAFT; Gao et al. 2020 (RobustTAD) report significant anomaly-detection gains from APP combined with time-domain methods. It preserves the amplitude spectrum, which is why it damages seasonality less than time warping does.

**Mixup for forecasting** has essentially no independent evidence outside the TSFM pretraining papers. Chronos's TSMixup is the reference implementation and its own ablation says the in-domain gain is nil. Moirai-2 reused it at scale (30M series, 63B obs) for **pretraining**. Nobody reports mixup helping a single-domain forecasting fine-tune.

**Does augmentation help more in the small-data regime? Yes, but weakly and inconsistently.** Iwana & Uchida §7.2.1, verbatim:

> "We expect the correlation to be negative because larger datasets are known to already generalize well. In other words, **data augmentation should have a larger effect on smaller datasets**… For most model and data augmentation pairs, our expectation is confirmed. **ResNet and LSTM-FCN especially have strong negative correlations** for most of the methods… **However, for some methods, such as Scaling with MLP and LSTM, there is a positive correlation** and for many others, there is almost no correlation. Thus, **for many models, such as MLP, LSTM, and BLSTM, training set size is not a strong indicator for improvement in accuracy**."

They also find a **positive** correlation between Δ-accuracy and *dataset variance*: augmentation helps most when patterns are already diverse, and hurts when they are tight — *"datasets with small variations have similar patterns, even between classes, and would be disturbed from the transformations."* That is directly relevant to a single-domain corpus, which is by construction low-variance.

### 6b. Heterogeneous sampling rates and units — five different answers

| Model | Sampling rate | Units / scale |
|---|---|---|
| **Chronos** | **Ignored entirely.** *"Perhaps counter-intuitively, in Chronos, we ignore time and frequency information, treating the 'time series' simply as a sequence."* No date features. | Mean scaling (`x/mean|x|`), chosen because *"it preserves zero values… which are often semantically meaningful"*. Then uniform binning into 4096 tokens over [−15, +15]. |
| **Moirai** | **Multiple patch sizes bound to frequency** — 5 input + 5 output projections over patch sizes {8,16,32,64,128}, mapped by a hard-coded heuristic. Removing it is the paper's largest ablation loss (+76.5% MAE). | Non-learnable RevIN + a **mixture output distribution** (Student's t / negative binomial / log-normal / low-variance normal) to absorb residual heterogeneity. |
| **TimesFM** | Granularity-balanced sampling + **per-granularity context caps** (512 / 256 weekly / 64 monthly+). Synthetic data patches under-represented frequencies. | RevIN standardization from the **first input patch** only. |
| **MOMENT** | **Ignored** — *"often unavailable outside of time series forecasting datasets."* Fixed T=512 for everything. | RevIN per instance, strict channel independence, `[MASK]` for any patch with a missing step, zero left-pad for short series. |
| **TTM** | **Both, explicitly:** *adaptive patching* (patch length varies by backbone level) **+** *resolution prefix tuning* (each resolution → an integer → a learnable embedding prefix), **+ DRS** (synthesize downsampled copies to rebalance the corpus). | Standard instance norm. DRS exists specifically because *"high-resolution datasets will account for a larger fraction of the samples… this can lead to a model that is **biased toward the finer resolution data**."* |
| **Lag-Llama** | **Implicit** — date-time covariates from second-of-minute up to quarter-of-year; all but one are constant step-to-step for a given series, so the model infers the frequency. | Per-window scaler; μ and σ appended as summary-statistic features. |

TTM's RPT is the only technique in this list with a measured benefit specifically for **short contexts** (+8%), and TTM's DRS is the only rebalancing device with a measured effect (+30%).

### 6c. Contamination screening — this is the strongest section of the literature and the weakest part of practice

**The lineage audit.** arXiv 2510.13654 ("Rethinking Evaluation in the Era of Time Series Foundation Models: (Un)known Information Leakage Challenges") traced the dataset lineage of **22 peer-reviewed TSFMs** published through January 2026:

> "Once a dataset has been used for pre-training or fine-tuning by any model, it must be regarded as contaminated and is no longer admissible for TSFM benchmarking… **only 6% of the analyzed datasets have never been used for pre-training or fine-tuning**, making them the only suitable candidates for genuine zero-shot model benchmarking."

They also document why name-matching is insufficient: *"'Elecdemand' from the Monash Repository is a scaled subset (1/1000) of the 'Australian Electricity Demand' dataset"*; ElectricityLoadDiagrams20112014 appears as "Electricity" in Autoformer/Monash and "ECL" in Informer; the same ride-share data appears in both Monash and GluonTS.

**How much leakage is worth.** GIFT-Eval (arXiv 2410.10393) App. F.2 is the canonical ablation — they pretrained Moirai on their clean split and compared against the original Moirai whose corpus contained ~0.1% of the eval data:

> "**In most cases, data leakage from training sets can boost performance on the corresponding test sets, with this effect becoming more pronounced as prediction length increases.** This finding highlights the **capacity of foundation models to memorize training data**."

Re-analysed in 2510.13654: at short horizons the leaked model has on average **7.6 percentage points lower MAPE**; at medium horizons **32 pp**; at long horizons **29 pp**. And **larger models are more susceptible** — the biggest gap is Moirai-L vs Moirai-Leakage-L.

**Indirect leakage — the one that will actually bite you.** 2510.13654 §3.2 identifies a failure mode specific to globally-trained models: *"if training and test series **overlap temporally and have a causal relationship** (confounding or direct causation), such pattern transfer can result in information leakage."* Two measurements:

- **Rodrigo & Ortiz (2024):** metro, bus, road and train usage in Madrid, 2024. Two globally-trained models, both predicting only the held-out metro test period. Model A had a common train/test cut across all series; model B cut only the metro series and kept the *other correlated series whole* in training. **MAE 439.14 (clean) vs 248.24 (leaky) — a 43.47% improvement from indirect leakage alone**, with no direct access to the target series.
- **Their own replication** with a from-scratch Time-Series Transformer: only **7 series out of 484 (1,600 of 205,859 observations = 0.78%)** temporally overlapped the COVID test window. The leaky model still won 8 of 10 seeds, with **up to ~37% MAE difference during the shock**.

**Their recommended standard** (§4) is two-dimensional, and it is exactly the standard I'd hold your corpus to:

> "Unlike local models, TSFMs learn patterns globally. Consequently, **strict temporal ordering within a single time series is no longer sufficient** to guarantee a fair evaluation… **if the last pre-training timestamp across all evaluated models is t, only observations from t+1 onwards can be present in the test set.**"

**Current practice.** fev-bench (arXiv 2509.26468) reports a per-model **self-reported Leakage (%)** column — in Chronos-2's Table 3: Moirai-2.0 **28%**, TimesFM-2.5 **8%**, Toto-1.0 **8%**, TiRex 1%, Sundial 1%, and Chronos-2 / Chronos-Bolt / TabPFN-TS / COSMIC / the statistical baselines **0%**. GIFT-Eval ships a dedicated *non-leaking* pretraining corpus: **71 univariate + 17 multivariate datasets, 7 domains, 13 frequencies, 4.5M series, ~230B data points**, against a 28-dataset / 144K-series / 177M-point evaluation set. TabPFN-TS's structural answer — pretrain on synthetic only — makes contamination *impossible*, which is why it can make the claim it does.

### 6d. Marginal value of an extra source vs an extra augmentation

**Almost nobody measures this directly. Two papers come close, and they disagree in an instructive way.**

- **TTM is the only clean measurement.** DRS (resolution augmentation of existing datasets) = **+30%** zero-shot. Going 250M → 1B samples by **adding a whole new archive** (LibCity) = **+6%**. On their setup, augmentation beat a new source by 5×. Their own gloss: *"while the quantity of pre-training data is significant, the **quality** of the data, especially in terms of **resolution diversity and coverage**, is even more crucial."*
- **Moirai measures the source side only.** "w/o LOTSA" (Monash+GluonTS only, ~27× less data) costs **+23.5% MAE**, and the paper attributes it to *diversity*, not volume — but the experiment cannot separate the two.
- **Chronos measures the augmentation side only**, and finds the in-domain gain is zero (Figure 10a) with a zero-shot gain that saturates at 10% synthetic (Figure 10b).
- **Moirai-2's ablation** gives the cleanest single number for "swap the corpus, hold everything else": **−8.5% MASE / −10.4% CRPS**, the second-largest step in their whole ablation ladder.

Nobody has run the head-to-head you actually want (add one source vs add one augmentation, matched budget, same model). Say so; it is a real gap.

---

## 7. The transfer question — answered explicitly

I read your `db_route` pipeline to answer this concretely rather than generically. Your setup: **`DEFAULT_TARGET = 3000` entities × M=5 anchors = ~15,000 samples**; entities are (service group, station) pairs over a six-region catchment from `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` (CC-BY-4.0); 6–10 signal channels per sample; four sibling profiles S/M/L/XM differing only in context length; targets `departure_delay_min` and `late_5min` (18.9%–28% positive); model is OpenTSLM (arXiv 2510.02410), LoRA on an LLM backbone with a time-series encoder.

### What does not transfer — be blunt about this

**TSMixup does not transfer, and its own ablation says so.** Three independent reasons:

1. **Chronos measured the in-domain effect and it was nil.** *"The model trained on TSMixup augmentations obtains **similar in-domain performance** to the model trained without augmentations. However, the **zero-shot** performance improves."* Your evaluation is entirely in-domain. You would be buying the one thing you don't need.
2. **The mechanism requires cross-dataset diversity you don't have.** Algorithm 1 line 6 samples a *dataset index* uniformly from N_d=28 datasets. With one archive, N_d = 1, and TSMixup degenerates into averaging pairs of German rail delay series — which is not a new pattern, it is a smoothed old one. Iwana & Uchida's variance correlation (§7.2.4) predicts exactly this: augmentation helps least when the dataset variance is low.
3. **It would break your label.** Your labels are functions of `(entity, anchor)` and your `assert_no_horizon_leak` invariant depends on that binding. A convex combination of two entities' histories has no coherent target, no coherent `ctx_*` slot, and no defensible rationale text. You would have to fabricate a label for it, and the resulting sample would teach the model to hallucinate.

**KernelSynth does not transfer either, for a different reason.** Its measured job in TimesFM was **frequency coverage** — *"there is almost no difference between the two models on the hourly ETTh datasets which has a well represented granularity"*. You have one archive at fixed resolutions you control. There is no under-represented frequency for GP samples to fill. And note the optimum in Chronos was **10%** with performance degrading above it — at your scale, 10% of 15,000 is 1,500 GP samples, which is far too few to change a 1B-parameter LoRA fine-tune and far too many to be harmless if they're off-distribution.

**The Salesforce synthetic-data survey (arXiv 2503.11411) states the position directly.** Its TSFM section has subsections for synthetic data in *pretraining* and in *evaluation* — and **no fine-tuning subsection at all**. Its §3.3 lists this as an open problem:

> "**Missed Opportunity to Finetune with Synthetic Data.** The focus on synthetic data has almost exclusively been on **pretraining**, while finetuning **remains an untapped potential**. After a TSFM is pretrained, finetuning with carefully designed synthetic data could serve as a precise intervention…"

So: synthetic augmentation for a single-domain fine-tune is not a proven technique the field endorses. It is a **stated research direction with no published evidence behind it**. If you do it, you are running the experiment, not applying a result. That is a defensible thing to say to a jury — and a much better answer than pretending Chronos validated it.

**Also irrelevant at your scale:** LOTSA's ε=0.001 sub-dataset cap (you have one dataset), TimesFM's granularity buckets (you fixed your resolutions), Moirai's per-frequency patch projections (OpenTSLM has one patch size, 4), and every observation-count figure in sections 1–5. Do not let anyone anchor you to 84B or 27B; those are pretraining budgets for a different problem.

---

# The framing that decides the ranking

Your delay-cause codes are the IRIS `<m>` message codes. Here is the actual table (from `derf/Travel-Status-DE-IRIS`, `lib/Travel/Status/DE/IRIS/Result.pm` — DB does not publish it):

| Theme | Codes already in your data |
|---|---|
| Weather | 11 Unwetter · 22 Witterungsbedingte Beeinträchtigungen · 53 Unwetterauswirkungen · 59 Schnee und Eis · 60 Witterungsbedingt verminderte Geschwindigkeit · 65 Erdrutsch · 66 Hochwasser |
| Strike | 9 Streikauswirkungen · 52 Streik |
| Construction | 31 Bauarbeiten · 35 Streckensperrung · 42 Außerplanmäßige Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkung · 54 Verfügbarkeit der Gleise eingeschränkt · 58 Umleitung |
| Crowding | 68 Hohes Fahrgastaufkommen · 32 Längere Haltezeit am Bahnhof |
| Knock-on | 43 Verspätung eines vorausfahrenden Zuges · 48 Verspätung aus vorheriger Fahrt · 44 · 47 · 51 |

**Every single one of your eight research topics is already a label in your corpus.** That cuts both ways, and which way decides everything:

- If cause codes are **features** → external weather/strike/works data is redundant. Don't bother.
- If cause codes are the **label** you predict (which they are — "cause explanation") → external data is the *only* thing available at inference time for those classes, because the code is revealed with or after the delay. Then weather is a legitimate predictor of the weather classes.

So the question is not "does weather help." It's "does weather help the cause head enough to matter, given the weather classes' base rate." **Run this before anything else** (5 minutes): count codes 11/22/53/59/60/65/66 as a share of coded stops in your corpus. If it's under ~1%, cap weather at 45 minutes and move on.

Two label-hygiene bugs worth more than any dataset below:
- **Codes 69–99 are comfort messages, not delay causes** (70 WLAN nicht verfügbar, 73 Heute: Mehrzweckabteil vorne, 77 1. Klasse fehlt, 80 Abweichende Wagenreihung). If they're in your label space, drop them.
- **Code 23 (`Betriebsstabilisierung`) was deleted on 2025-12-14** — a taxonomy change *inside your window*.

---

# Correction to your premise: your corpus is bigger than 10 months, but not usefully so

I verified this directly against the parquet files:

| File | Rows | Distinct stations |
|---|---|---|
| `data-2024-08.parquet` | 1,888,035 | **109** |
| `data-2025-10.parquet` | 1,989,180 | **107** |
| `data-2025-11.parquet` | 13,943,561 | **5,293** |
| `data-2026-02.parquet` | 13,721,520 | **5,304** |

The upstream README states it plainly: *"Data of the biggest ~100 stations is available from 2024-07 to 2025-11-02 and since then until now for all stations."*

So your 10 months **is** the full-coverage era (2025-11-02 → now, 26 monthly files, 7.74 GB total). There are 16 extra months available but only at ~107 stations (~32M extra rows). That's not nothing — it adds **winter 2024/25** and **Oktoberfest 2024 and 2025** at exactly the busy hubs — but a naive concat creates a station-coverage regime change mid-corpus that will wreck a time-based split. Cost: ~30 min, and only worth it if you specifically want a second winter.

Three more caveats from the same README that will bite you:
- **All timestamps are Europe/Berlin local (CET/CEST), not UTC.** This is the single most likely way a weather join silently fails.
- Missing hours from API errors: 2025-11: 6h · 2026-02: 7h · 2026-03: 10h · 2026-04: 34h · 2026-05: 31h · 2026-06: 6h · **2026-07: 102h**.

## 1. Join hub + label hygiene — 45 min, do this first

Nobody asked for this and it's the highest-value item. One 7.5 MB file solves *four* of your joins at once:

```
https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/db-stations@latest/full.json
```

ISC licence, no auth, **5,388 stations, 100% coverage** on every field I checked:

| Field | Unlocks |
|---|---|
| `id` (EVA) | joins straight to your `eva` column |
| `location.latitude/longitude` | → nearest DWD station (**weather**) |
| `ril100` (DS100) | → InfraGO Streckennummer + km (**infrastructure**) |
| `federalState` | → per-Bundesland school/public holidays (**calendar**) |
| `category` (1–7) + `weight` | → station-size / footfall proxy (**crowding**) |

Category distribution: 1:24 · 2:84 · 3:275 · 4:641 · 5:973 · 6:2,496 · 7:895. `weight` tops out at Nürnberg Hbf 1121.2, Köln Hbf 1043.3, München Hbf 1034.6, München-Hackerbrücke 629.5.

You have StaDa credentials and could get most of this from the API, but this is instant and offline.

## 2. Upstream-delay features — 1–1.5 h, no external data

DB's own taxonomy tells you this is where the mass is: codes **43** (delay of a preceding train) and **48** (delay inherited from the previous run) are core reactionary causes, and the delay-prediction literature is consistent that *delay at the preceding station is the strongest single predictor*, with the previous two stations in the top five features.

You already have `train_line_ride_id` and `train_line_station_num` — that's a ready-made trip sequence. Build:
- delay of the same train at stop *n−1* and *n−2*
- delay of the previous train to call at this station (same platform/direction if you can infer it)
- rolling median delay at this station over the last 60 min
- scheduled dwell = `departure_planned_time − arrival_planned_time`, and slack to the next stop

If you do exactly one thing from this whole document, do this one. It will outperform every external join below combined.

## 3. Timetable-sparsity feature — 30 min, no external data

`planned_stops_per_station_hour ÷ 28-day rolling median for that (station, hour, weekday)`.

Because DB loads emergency/construction timetables into the published plan ahead of time, this one derived column captures strikes, storm plans, Streckensperrungen and Baustellen simultaneously — with no external feed, no licence and no history problem. It is strictly better than the strike calendar and better than any baustellen feed you cannot get.

## 4. Calendar — 45 min

**Use OpenHolidays, not ferien-api.** One API for both holiday types, per-Bundesland, data ODbL-1.0 (API code AGPL-3.0), German data 2012→2028, no documented rate limit, ~12 requests total:

```
https://openholidaysapi.org/PublicHolidays?countryIsoCode=DE&languageIsoCode=DE&validFrom=2025-11-01&validTo=2026-12-31&subdivisionCode=DE-BY
https://openholidaysapi.org/SchoolHolidays?countryIsoCode=DE&languageIsoCode=DE&validFrom=2025-11-01&validTo=2026-12-31&subdivisionCode=DE-BY
```

Codes: `DE-BY DE-BE DE-HH DE-NW DE-HE DE-BW` for your six.

**7 of 16 public holidays differ across your six regions** — Heilige Drei Könige (BY, BW), Internationaler Frauentag (BE), Fronleichnam (BY, NW, HE, BW), Augsburger Friedensfest (Augsburg only), Mariä Himmelfahrt (BY Catholic Gemeinden), Reformationstag (HH), Allerheiligen (BY, NW, BW). So a per-Bundesland flag genuinely beats a national one.

School holidays give far more: over 2025–2026 there are **399 days where at least one of your six regions is on holiday but only 41 where all six are** — 358 days of cross-region contrast. Frankfurt and Munich's 2026 summer holidays are ~5 weeks apart.

Highest-signal encoding, and it isn't `is_holiday`: **`days_to_school_holiday_start` and `days_from_school_holiday_end`, clipped to ±3, per region.** The Friday/Saturday starting a Bundesland's Sommerferien is the German rail peak day, and because the Länder are staggered it rolls across your six regions on six different weekends.

Also nearly free and nobody else will have it: **Fahrplanwechsel**. The annual timetable change is 2024-12-15, **2025-12-14** (inside your window), 2026-12-13. The two weeks after reliably run worse.

`ferien-api.de` is alive (MIT) but its end dates are padded to the weekend — one day later than OpenHolidays. KMK publishes only PDFs and .ics; don't scrape them.

## 5. Network topology / infrastructure — 2–3 h, and the best external dataset that exists

This is the real find. Free, CC-BY 4.0, no auth, no registration — I verified the download returns HTTP 200 with `Content-Disposition: attachment`:

```
https://mobilithek.info/mdp-api/files/aux/922109165921083392/Infrastrukturdaten.zip   # 27.9 MB
https://mobilithek.info/mdp-api/files/aux/922109165921083392/Infrastrukturdaten.gpkg  # same, GeoPackage
```

(This is a Mobilithek *aux file* — a plain anonymous GET, so your "Mobilithek ruled out for approval friction" decision doesn't apply. Note the GovData catalogue prints these with a **double** slash after the host, which 404s into an HTML shell. Use the single slash above.)

Done on both fronts. Tests: **147 passed**.

## The yield problem — fixed

9/180 → **148/150 usable records** at both S and XM. It was never a data gap; all four causes were accounting errors about what an empty bucket means:

| Cause | Killed | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `works_share` *interpolated* across buckets with no attributed delay | 63/146 | Zero-imputed — "nothing blamed on works" is a fact, `attributed_share` keeps zero unambiguous |
| Station's open hours judged every grain | 45/146 | Per-grain denominators: new `service_throughput` channel; pair = both intersected |
| XM's coarse layers had no count channel at all | 91/150 XM | Both count channels ride every layer |
| Nov–Jan anchors reached back past the 2025-11-02 coverage expansion | 44/44 | Anchor window starts 120 d after — the plan's "L-limited shared anchor set" rule |
| `Bus` (rail-replacement, 336k events/mo) qualified as a train entity | — | Excluded as entity, kept in station throughput |

`service_at_station_delay` moved to the 6h/daily layers only — at hourly it's ~93% empty *by timetable*. Shapes now: S 7 series, M 10, L 10, XM 19 / 834 patches. Uncommitted on `feat/db-route-multiscale`.

## The research, consolidated

I stopped the one agent still running and read the other reports' transcripts myself. Full brief: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/da3c582a-9bf6-42be-8038-f142c168cac9**

**What OpenTSLM did, mainly:** the repo has *no data-construction code* — every loader downloads a finished CSV from an ETH polybox share. Measured from the files: **zero augmentation, zero synthetic data of their own** (TSQA is third-party), a 5-stage sequential curriculum with no replay and no ablation, Sleep-CoT is 6 recordings randomly split so every test subject is in train, 2,536 ECG rationales end in the wrong answer, 706 M4 captions are literally `Error generating caption: Connection error.` Their best dataset was their smallest (7,434 rows). The one transferable trick — z-score then re-inject mean/std as text — our bridge already does.

**Frontier models (Chronos/MOIRAI/TimesFM):** TSMixup and KernelSynth are pretraining tricks; Chronos measured TSMixup's *in-domain* gain at nil, and synthetic *hurts* past ~10%. Nobody has published evidence that synthetic data helps a single-domain fine-tune.

**What actually transfers:**
1. A fresh entity is worth **12.5×** a sixth anchor — breadth over depth; six regions was the right call.
2. **Chronos-2 as frozen encoder**: +17 F1 on Gemma-270M in their own Table 3 — bigger than any augmentation result in the literature.
3. **Run a gradient-boosting baseline** on the `ctx_*` scalars — we're above every measured break-even and a jury will ask.
4. Cap `REPEAT_MAX` at 2 (exact duplication → memorisation).

**More data, ranked:** the top three need no new source — upstream-delay features from the run sequence (`lag2_delay` is 74× the next feature in the Dutch study), a timetable-sparsity channel, a station join hub. Then holidays, then DB InfraGO infrastructure (free CC-BY, includes the legally-declared congested lines). Weather: thin version, cause-head only. Crowding/concerts/fairs: dead.

Next on my side: the connector package + `timenet-build` — the actual card deliverable.

"""The :class:`BaseConnector` contract every dataset integration implements.

A connector fetches raw data and converts it into a :class:`~timenet.dataset.TimeFDataset`. It has no
knowledge of the registry, engine, or any other connector. The engine drives it
``download -> convert``, then stores the result itself. The consumer SDK never imports connector
code: it builds only through the ``timenet.builders`` entry point.
"""

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import asyncio
import inspect
from pathlib import Path
from typing import ClassVar, Generic, TypeVar

from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset
from timenet.types import DatasetMetadata


TRaw = TypeVar("TRaw")


class BaseConnector(ABC, Generic[TRaw]):
    """Abstract base for dataset connectors. One concrete subclass per dataset.

    A connector lives in its own folder and declares its descriptive identity in a ``dataset.yaml``
    card beside it (read by :meth:`metadata`). Set :attr:`CARD` to point elsewhere. Subclasses
    implement the two abstract stages. ``download`` is I/O-only and ``convert`` is CPU-only.
    Connectors take no constructor arguments.
    """

    __test__ = False  # a connector named Test* (for example, the test_mean dataset) is not a pytest test class

    CARD: ClassVar[str | Path | None] = None
    """Optional explicit path to the dataset card YAML. When ``None`` (the default), the connector
    reads the card from ``dataset.yaml`` in its own folder."""

    values_backend: str = "parquet"
    """Default storage backend for this connector's values plane."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        cls = type(self)
        # download() is concrete because it bridges to download_async. A subclass that overrides
        # neither would instantiate and only fail deep in the engine. Catch it at construction instead.
        if cls.download is BaseConnector.download and cls.download_async is BaseConnector.download_async:
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must implement download() or download_async()")

    @classmethod
    def _card_path(cls) -> Path:
        """Resolve the dataset card path by convention.

        Returns:
            :attr:`CARD` if set, otherwise ``dataset.yaml`` in the directory of the connector's module.
        """
        if cls.CARD is not None:
            return Path(cls.CARD)
        return Path(inspect.getfile(cls)).with_name("dataset.yaml")

    def metadata(self) -> DatasetMetadata:
        """Return the dataset's descriptive identity, loaded and validated from its card YAML.

        Reads the card by convention (``dataset.yaml`` beside the connector, unless :attr:`CARD`
        overrides it). Its ``dataset_id`` must match the id used to register or build the connector.

        Returns:
            The dataset's :class:`~timenet.types.DatasetMetadata`.
        """
        return DatasetMetadata.from_yaml(self._card_path())

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]:
        """Fetch or discover raw source files and return lightweight references to them.

        I/O only: no parsing, no array work. Must be idempotent for a given ``cache_dir``. Override
        this for a synchronous connector. For an I/O-bound one, override :meth:`download_async`
        instead and leave this default, which drives it to completion, since the engine calls
        connectors synchronously.

        Args:
            cache_dir: Directory to write downloaded files into (created by the engine).

        Returns:
            Raw references passed directly to :meth:`convert`.
        """
        return asyncio.run(self.download_async(cache_dir))

    async def download_async(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]:
        """Async variant of :meth:`download` for connectors whose downloads are I/O-bound.

        Override this to fetch artifacts concurrently, for example with the connector HTTP download
        helpers. The default :meth:`download` runs it for you. Implement exactly one of the two.

        Args:
            cache_dir: Directory to write downloaded files into (created by the engine).

        Returns:
            Raw references passed directly to :meth:`convert`.

        Raises:
            NotImplementedError: If a subclass overrides neither :meth:`download` nor
                :meth:`download_async`.
        """

            "a connector must implement download() (synchronous) or download_async() (asynchronous)"
        )

    @abstractmethod
    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[TRaw]) -> TimeFDataset:
        """Parse raw references and populate a :class:`~timenet.dataset.TimeFDataset`.

        CPU-bound: no network I/O. Attach time-series values as lazy loaders instead of materializing
        them.

        Args:
            raw_refs: The references returned by :meth:`download`.

        Returns:
            The populated dataset.
        """

"""Builder discovery: how the SDK finds something able to build a dataset the registry lacks.

The SDK cannot import a connectors package (the dependency runs the other way), so a build
backend registers itself under the ``timenet.builders`` entry-point group instead. This keeps the
SDK's whole knowledge of building to one protocol and one lookup, and lets a third-party connector
package plug in the same way the first-party one does.
"""

from importlib.metadata import entry_points
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Protocol


ENTRY_POINT_GROUP = "timenet.builders"


class BuilderBackend(Protocol):
    """Something that can build a dataset from its connector."""

    def knows(self, dataset_id: str) -> bool:
        """Report whether this backend has a connector for the id.

        Implementations must answer without importing the connector: this runs before any
        connector environment exists.

        Args:
            dataset_id: The dataset id.

        Returns:
            Whether the backend can build it.
        """
        ...

    def declared_version(self, dataset_id: str) -> str | None:
        """Return the version the connector declares, without importing or building it.

        A caller checks a version pin against this before the build runs, so a pin the connector
        cannot satisfy fails fast instead of after a full build. Answer without importing the
        connector, like :meth:`knows`.

        Args:
            dataset_id: The dataset id.

        Returns:
            The declared version string, or ``None`` if it cannot be read.
        """
        ...

    def build(self, dataset_id: str, root: Path, *, force: bool = False) -> Path:
        """Build the dataset into a registry directory.

        Args:
            dataset_id: The dataset id.
            root: The output registry directory.
            force: Rebuild even if the version is already built.

        Returns:
            The committed version directory.
        """
        ...


def find_builder(dataset_id: str) -> BuilderBackend | None:
    """Return the first registered backend that claims this dataset id.

    Args:
        dataset_id: The dataset id.

    Returns:
        The backend, or ``None`` when no installed package claims the id.
    """
    for entry in entry_points(group=ENTRY_POINT_GROUP):
        backend = entry.load()()
        if backend.knows(dataset_id):
            return backend
    return None

## A.4 What a connector is, and how to write one

### A.4.1 The contract — `packages/timenet/src/timenet/connectors/base.py`

```python
class BaseConnector(ABC, Generic[TRaw]):
    CARD: ClassVar[str | Path | None] = None
    values_backend: str = "parquet"

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        cls = type(self)
        if cls.download is BaseConnector.download and cls.download_async is BaseConnector.download_async:
            raise TypeError(f"{cls.__name__} must implement download() or download_async()")

    @classmethod
    def _card_path(cls) -> Path:
        if cls.CARD is not None:
            return Path(cls.CARD)
        return Path(inspect.getfile(cls)).with_name("dataset.yaml")

    def metadata(self) -> DatasetMetadata:            # CONCRETE — do not override
        return DatasetMetadata.from_yaml(self._card_path())

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]:     # I/O only, idempotent, no parsing
        return asyncio.run(self.download_async(cache_dir))

    async def download_async(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[TRaw]: ...   # override ONE of the two

    @abstractmethod
    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[TRaw]) -> TimeFDataset: ...  # CPU only, no network
```

| Method | Nature | Contract |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `download(cache_dir)` | I/O only | Fetch or find raw files and return lightweight references. Idempotent, does not parse data. |
| `convert(raw_refs)` | CPU only | Parse references into a `TimeFDataset` with **lazy Arrow loaders**. Does not use the network. |

Also concrete (inherited, rarely overridden): `store()` — derives the schema if missing and streams through `TimeFWriter`, returning the committed version directory.

**Connectors take no constructor arguments.** Configuration comes from environment variables read in `__init__`.

### A.4.2 Registration = folder convention, no central registry

From `docs/connectors.md` + `discovery.py`:

```
packages/timenet-connectors/src/timenet_connectors/datasets/<org>/<name>/
  __init__.py       # re-exports CONNECTOR (and the class) from connector.py
  connector.py      # the BaseConnector subclass; ends with CONNECTOR = <YourClass>
  dataset.yaml      # the dataset card, read by metadata()
  requirements.txt  # optional; libs installed into the build's isolated env
  tests/            # fixture-based, offline
```

> The system finds connectors lazily, by dataset id. **There is no central registry to maintain.**

`discovery._module_name` maps the id: **org lowercased, leaf hyphens → underscores**. So `physionet/ecg-qa-cot` → `...datasets.physionet.ecg_qa_cot/`. `connector_dir()` is deliberately import-free (uses `find_spec`) and requires a `dataset.yaml` to be present, which is how an org namespace package is distinguished from a real connector.

### A.4.3 Reusable bases

**`BaseHuggingFaceConnector`** (`bases/huggingface.py`) — you implement **only** `convert`:

```python
class BaseHuggingFaceConnector(BaseConnector[dict[str, Any]], ABC):
    HF_REPO: ClassVar[str]
    PARQUET_REVISION: ClassVar[str] = "refs/convert/parquet"
    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:  # inherited: one dict per row
```

It reads the Hub's **auto-converted parquet branch**, so any source format (CSV/JSON/…) is handled uniformly, without depending on `datasets`. `HF_TOKEN` is read from the env for gated repos. Fully private repos have no auto-parquet ref and are **not supported**.

**`BasePhysioNetConnector`** (`bases/physionet.py`) — you implement `download` + `convert`:

```python
class WfdbHeader(NamedTuple):
    fs: float; sig_len: int; sig_name: list[str]
    dat_names: tuple[str, ...]; formats: tuple[str, ...]
    gains: tuple[float, ...]; baselines: tuple[int, ...]; direct_read: bool

@staticmethod
def _read_header(record_base: Path) -> WfdbHeader: ...
def _lead_loader(self, record_base: Path, header: WfdbHeader, lead_idx: int) -> Callable[[], pa.Array]: ...
```

It parses `.hea` text directly (bypassing `wfdb.rdheader`'s pandas DataFrame, "those millions of scalar lookups otherwise dominate a large convert") and reads format-16 `.dat` files with `np.fromfile` + an LRU cache so all leads of a record read the file once. Falls back to `wfdb.rdsamp` for other formats.

**Download helpers** (`timenet_connectors.download`):

```python
await download_files([Artifact(url, dest, headers=?, cookies=?, sha256=?), ...],
```
